speakerposition: N.D.P. Deputy House Leader
subtopic: CARRIAGE OF GOODS BY WATER ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too am pleased to rise on behalf of my colleagues with respect to Bill C-83, the carriage of goods by water act. This bill tabled by the government provides for the
Minister of Transport to report to the House of Commons on the advisability of replacing the existing Hague-Visby rules with the Hamburg rules. That action would take place prior to December 31, 1999.
I want to say that the NDP transport critic, the member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan, is unable to be here today. Nevertheless he was instrumental in the process that led up to the debate we are having today. He suggested to the committee and was able to convince the Standing Committee on Transport which reviewed this bill to change it to require the report by the minister be automatically forwarded to the Standing Committee on Transport and the committee have the power to "undertake a review of the minister's report and the committee shall report its findings back to the House including a statement on the advisability of enacting the Hamburg rules".
While to most people this change would seem to be an extremely minor one, it is part of the broader issue which I am also interested in of giving additional powers and responsibilities to standing committees.
Too often the standing committee is excluded from the decision-making process. While from time to time ministers refer specific matters to a standing committee, such as the white paper on freedom to move and deregulation and the National Transportation Agency Review Commission report, as another one that comes to mind, at other times the committee itself decides to embark on a review of a policy matter such as the VIA Rail cuts, high speed rail, or the St. Lawrence Seaway, for example. Nevertheless there is still a broad range of policy decision making that standing committees have not been involved in. This is one more way of involving the standing committee in a meaningful way in the policymaking process.
Many bills passed by the House have a mandatory review provision built into them. In some cases the review occurs after the act has been in place for five years like the WGTA or three years like the Transportation Safety Board. In these cases the government appoints an independent commission to conduct the work.

The NTA review commission, which was just recently completed, cost the taxpayers millions of dollars. There are those of us who believe that the Standing Committee on Transport which reviewed the original policy paper, Freedom to Move and the enabling legislation, could have done the job of the five-year review at considerably lower cost to the taxpayer and, I might say, I think with different conclusions.
The same argument could be made for the now under way review of the Transportation Safety Board Act being conducted only three years after the act was passed. The transport committee helped create the new board through its work in reviewing the original act and they could be charged with the task of seeing how well that act is working.
In any event what we have before us today is a small step for the transport committee and for parliamentary reform in so far as it affects the committee, but it is one that we are happy to see.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to rise in this House to speak on Bill C-83.
This act respecting the transportation of goods by water which was referred to the transport committee has brought to light an issue that ought to be pointed out in
this debate at report stage. Through the transport committee, we could, without prejudice to efficiency, with members who are interested in transportation, allow this committee to get more involved in terms of recommendations and encourage government to pay attention to these recommendations.
For one thing, the transport committee could very well do the work that independent commissions are set up for. Independent commissions are created right and left to make recommendations to government, and then these recommendations are implemented, be it in transportation or other areas. What if, to save money in these recessionary times, government decided to pay more attention-which I think it did indeed in this bill-to the input from the transport committee? Then, the legislative committees could recommend that such and such amendment or item be examined at the transport committee level. This way, instead of spending thousands of dollars on independent commissions, the government could use the money to let parliamentarians-because there would not just be members of Parliament involved-play a much more interesting part in this process.
Members of Parliament, especially those with no direct connection to cabinet, regularly complain about not being involved in the decision-making process. And this is true of members on both side of this House. This is a fine example of them actually playing an active part in developing recommendations. The same should be done at the standing committee level to develop recommendations that would be taken into account by government and save the cost of independent commissions-we are talking about millions of dollars here-which end up duplicating the recommendations from the standing committee and then, in many instances, the recommendations are shelved for years.
A major point to bear in mind while debating this bill, as the NDP spokesperson pointed out, is the renewal of some legislation after five years. That colleague was saying that, instead of relying on an independent commission to renew the act for five years, the Committee on Transport could, during its regular work, make that recommendation and thus avoid duplication. God knows there is a lot of duplication here in the House of Commons, as well as in provincial legislatures, which is very unfortunate. It is necessary in times of economic

We say in this bill that we must review transport safety every three years. Well, all the boards that are being set up could be monitored by the Committee on Transport instead of independent commissions hired by contract to submit recommendations.
I have an example in my riding of a lady, Mrs. Chaloux, whose husband unfortunately died at sea. She had to wait a year and a half before she got the safety report from the government.
It was during a meeting that I arranged for her and which took place on March 4 in Montreal that the board in question agreed to give her the safety report. Several people died, and in that area of the Lower St. Lawrence, several accidents happened.
The boards that are appointed and which make recommendations to us every three years are often not as close to the day-to-day reality of things that are happening in the transportation area than are members of Parliament, who have the feeling on their side, who sit on the Committee on Transport and are involved in it. It is an example that we must follow in the future business of the House and the committees. It seems to me that on the democratic road that will guide us for the years to come, there should be an incentive, even a commitment from the government to take into account the recommendations from the standing committees, such as the one on transport, and to reduce considerably the number of independent commissions and contracts that are awarded to them which often look like patronage to reward some friends of the party or to give a few contracts to lobbyists who are a little too annoying.
In that sense we are wasting the Canadian or Quebecer taxpayers' money by disregarding the role of members, their recommendations, their observations, their con-
Moreover, by involving members we would realize substantial savings. I repeat that this is duplication since members already do that work on the transport committee which makes recommendations so there is no point striking an independent commission to confirm the same thing. This belittles the role of hon. members. Conversely it is gratifying to be able to act, to be the focal point for the demands of our regions, and this is a role members want to play, especially those we call backbenchers. Committee members would feel that they are doing something useful. They would feel part of the democratic process of government. Moreover, this would save money and we know how badly the government wants to control spending.
The committee which worked on this is a good example of what I am saying. It came up with interesting recommendations. As mentioned earlier, the government spokesperson underlined the fact that we came up with some sort of consensus following transport committee hearings. Thanks to the efforts of all political parties involved, the committee was able to agree on recommendations.
I am glad, as a member of the Bloc Quebecois, to say that we are going to give our support to this bill which results from a real democratic reflection and involvement of all political parties. As was said earlier about the Hamburg rule, we had a greater involvement of members in committee, an enhanced role for the transport committee, a fact which in the future might pave the way for other recommendations and a similar role for other committees. I thank the hon. member for Longueuil, the transport critic, for allowing me to say a few words on this subject. Normally he would be the one to address the House on such important matters. He very kindly let me speak first, being the House leader, but I assume he will have his own comments to add as well, considering a public statement he made recently about Montreal's two airports.

Our critic also sat on the transport committee, and he was somewhat surprised to hear that Pearson was the only airport designated as national by the Minister of Transport, the others being considered regional airports.
Obviously a review is necessary. Our position is that we are here to defend the interests of Quebec in the House of Commons. The minister decided, for instance, to help Canadian and not Nationair. I think he was right, but he should have refused to help Canadian as well. However, these decisions should have been considered within the context of a comprehensive review of air transportation in Canada and of the entire transportation sector.
We want to defend the interests of Quebec here in the House of Commons in no uncertain terms. We feel that any policies being considered by the minister should include a comprehensive review of air transport and of the entire transportation sector in this country. For instance, he should have refused to help Canadian as he refused to help Nationair, which was the right decision.
Until there is a comprehensive review our critic will have some very interesting things to say and publish very shortly in the party platform the Bloc Quebecois is preparing for the next election campaign regarding the specific role we will play in this House in securing a return on the money we pay to the federal government.
As long as we pay taxes to Ottawa we will have a return on those taxes. This is vital in the transportation sector.
My transport critic pointed out the monumental mistake made by Parliament when it decided on the location of Mirabel airport. The highway link is no longer possible because it would now cost $150,000 to go under the runways.
They should have listened to the Government of Quebec and selected a site for the airport near Saint-Jean, Saint-Hyacinthe or Drummondville. It would have been in Quebec's economic heartland and the province's economic interests would have been well served. This was a monumental mistake.
I am not saying it was the present government's fault. This was done by the previous government but it is clear the present government is perpetuating, not correcting the mistakes made by the previous government. The
same applies to the deficit. The deficit was criticized for years, and now it has become intolerable. In fact, an initial deficit of $200 billion has now more than doubled under the Conservative government.
Basically nothing has changed. Increasingly Quebecers realize that they would be better off managing their own interests, their own money, both in the transportation sector and in other sectors. They would, of course, respect the rights of other Canadians and want to establish economic ties with the rest of Canada. Quebecers would like to see their taxes managed exclusively by the people and their elected representatives in the National Assembly and not by a government next door that redistributes taxes through equalization payments which it can freeze at any time, thus creating an imbalance of $700 or $800 million. This is what happened to Quebec during the past two years. The Quebec government had to take this shortfall and pass it on to the school boards and municipalities because it was not getting enough money from the federal government, equalization payments being frozen.
This is really too bad. We see this happening with equalization payments and we see the same thing in the transport sector. The Minister of Transport has sorely neglected the needs of the Montreal region. This coupled with poor decision making which has affected the transport sector in Quebec, has caused the Montreal region to suffer tremendous economic setbacks during the past ten years.
There is a pressing need for transferring authority in the transport and other sectors to Quebec's elected representatives. Under an economic union, we could have agreements reflecting the interests of the two countries that will soon constitute the territoiy still referred to today as Canada.
In conclusion I hope that hon. members will consider the committee's recommendations and that the report stage of Bill C-83 will be adopted as soon as possible. Very specific recommendations were made and an indepth study was conducted by the committees which considered the bill, including the transport committee. I think the NDP critic did an extremely good job on this committee. His comments and the amendments to the recommendations he suggested impressed most committee members.

This study on water transportation of goods will have an important impact in terms of safety-I mentioned earlier the case of Mrs. Chaloux-and in terms of better management of water transport without increasing the cost of that mode of transportation. Madam Speaker, I would like to ask a few questions and make some comments on the very good speech made by the hon. member for Richelieu- It is very good because it is a substantive speech.
We have three or four different modes of transport, whether it is by water, by air or by rail, and I have always deplored the fact that there are several governments involved in that area, whether municipal, provincial or federal, and so little common interest between the different governments or even within the federal department.
The big problem we see lies in a blatant lack of dialogue. Often, for example, water transport is supported to the detriment of rail transport or to the detriment of air transport and as a result governments spend money to promote air transport while subsidizing rail or water transports which compete between themselves. Governments spend money to promote one to the detriment of the other and then subsidize the other to the detriment of the first one. This becomes a kind of vicious circle wherein governments spend staggering
As we have seen the air and rail transport industries are faced with huge deficits mainly because of a lack of co-operation between the various levels of government.
When I was a government member, the member for Roberval, the then Minister of Transport, decided to cut down VTA's funding. I asked him if he had consulted with the public transit authorities in Montreal to see if some of the lines could be used for urban transit in the Montreal area. He said that matter did not come within his responsibility and that his only concern was with VIA. Since urban transit was an area of provincial jurisdiction it was not his problem.
When a minister shows very little interest in co-operating with other levels of government we have to realize that it is going to cost a bundle. That explains the present deficit which is $10 billion over the government's forecast for 1992.
That is absolutely unacceptable and that is why I have decided to take part in this debate today. The situation in the transportation industry is a real mess.
I would like to know if the hon. member for Richelieu agrees with me that there is a total lack of co-operation between the various transportation modes in Canada.

Madam Speaker, I see that the hon. member for Manicouagan seems quite interested by the nice comment just made by the hon. member for Longueuil, so much so in fact that I take his smile as applause. He does not want to disturb this House, even though this could be rather easily done, given the small number of members who seem to take an interest in this very important debate.
I want to thank the hon. member for Longueuil who, by pointing out what goes on at the municipal, provincial and federal levels, as well as with the different commissions, raised precisely the issue which I wanted to bring up, namely the duplication and the indescribable mess in the field of transport because of the number of offices.
This bill deals with the transportation of goods by sea.
I mentioned earlier the case where we had to wait for two years to get the results of an inquiry in the death of three or four people. This is unbelievable. The situation

is such because of the complexity of the administration of the different offices of the Department of Transport.
The situation is the same in the railroad sector. We discovered that a field where wheat had been sowed for 33 years still belonged, at least in part, to CN. It took 33 years before finally deciding to sell a strip of land the length of the House of Commons to the farmer who had been cultivating it for 33 years. This is an example of the mess to which the hon. member for Longueuil referred.
In my constituency there is a railway which they have just decided to abandon. The bridges linking the two regions of my riding fell 20 years ago and had never been repaired. Twenty years went by before deciding to abandon a line which was not used by any train. It took two and a half years to make the decision. The decision was made that long ago, but it will take another year before the land is transferred to owners along the railway. You can imagine the mess.
On the other hand, if the transport committee, as I said earlier, could make recommendations if not decisions which would be binding for the minister, it could ensure the review of each case of nonchalance by the offices and the various bodies which manage the transportation sector in Canada and particularly the transportation of goods by water. We are downgrading their services, considering them as insignificant safety officers on the same level as much lower officials. These officers have met every member of the House in the past month. Madam Speaker, as the Bloc Quebecois critic for transport I am pleased to rise today to speak on transport, and more specifically on marine transport.
I know that this bill is designed to improve the transportation of goods by water, to facilitate the berthing of our ships in small harbours, et cetera. I support this bill, but what concerns me most is the fact that once

Government Orders
again the government paid particular attention to transportation by water.
I am not convinced that the government took the necessary time to analyze the negative impact which the improvements made regarding transportation by water could have on the railroad industry.
As we are well aware, the CN chairman once again came to Ottawa this week. He appeared before the transport committee and he confirmed once again there would be an additional lay off of more than 1,000 employees at the CN.
We, members of the Bloc Quebecois, met the CP president a few months ago and he told us that the big problem for the railroad industry is the fact that shipping by sea is partly subsidized. So is transport by surface, since roads are built by governments, whereas railroad companies must build their railroads themselves. The costs incurred by railway companies are enormous, given the fact that they are in direct competition with the road transportation sector for which the roads are paid and insured by governments. This means that the railway companies are at a total disadvantage and this becomes totally unfair.
This is what I meant to say earlier. There is no consultation between the various transportation sectors in Canada and in Quebec. There is absolutely no consultation. Consequently governments subsidize some forms of transport to the detriment of others, which generates unfair competition and forces governments to pay and pay all the time. Transportation companies complain about this unfairness. Consequently the government decides to subsidize this transport sector, whether it is the rail, the marine or the air industry. This is a vicious circle in the sense that the government ends up paying all the time.
This is an obvious problem of bad management, and this is why I want to take this opportunity today to deal with the transport sector because this lack of consultation is totally unacceptable. I do not understand why people who are supposedly intelligent, educated and used to working in a industrialized country which is said to be number one in the world, cannot grasp this.
I also cannot understand why there are two airports in Montreal which are not operating successfully. I cannot understand why the government does not react. Also I never understood why, when Mirabel was built, the airport was north of the runways, while the population lives south of those runways. This is beyond me. I asked that question on several occasions to the transport committee in past years. As you know, Madam Speaker, this is my ninth year here as a member of Parliament, and I have had several opportunities to ask questions to the transport committee. I did ask why Mirabel airport was built north of the runways, while the population is located south of those runways. I never got much of an answer until about six months ago when experts provided one. I do not know if it is because I now sit with the opposition that I got an answer. I was told that when Mirabel was built it was first to serve the interests of Ottawa and Montreal. Autoroute 50 between Ottawa and Mirabel was supposed to be built, as well as autoroute 13 between Mirabel and Montreal, but the airport was built north of the runways to first serve Ottawa.
That is scandalous. Today highway 13 has still not been completed because it would cost $150 million to go under the runways, with the air terminal building located north of them.
That is completely unacceptable. I cannot understand it. I am an ordinary individual who does not know much. I am not an expert on transportation or economics but some things in life are just plain logical. This situation is beyond me.
I come back to my argument that transport should be managed by the Government of Quebec in the first place. As the old saying goes, you are never as well served as when you serve yourself. The day we are served by our Quebec government we will not put an airport in Mirabel to serve Ottawa instead of Montreal. That is what happened and I have proof. Experts finally admitted to me that Mirabel was built to serve Ottawa first.
I can tell you that Montrealers have had enough of the rivalry between these two airports. While traffic at Pearson Airport is growing, our Montreal airports are barely holding their own. According to the experts this

mess with two airports in Montreal costs the Quebec economy about $5 to $6 billion.
This leads me to say again that this lack of co-ordination among the modes of transport costs citizens and taxpayers huge amounts, exorbitantly high amounts for an outdated transportation system.
It is imperative that the federal, Quebec and municipal governments get together and agree on a comprehensive plan so that our marine, air, rail and truck transport can be profitable.
We know that transportation is one of the most important industries in Quebec, but the way it is managed in general is scandalous. I cannot understand how intelligent people can be that stupid.
With transportation everything is interrelated. People and goods have to be moved. Passengers travel by train, bus or car, by rail or by road. Encouraging transportation by road, for example, hurts the railway; encouraging transportation by rail hurts the bus lines.
We recently heard the Minister of Transport announce that he is restoring Via Rail service between Montreal and Quebec City.
That is very nice and the minister can boast that VIA Rail is running again between Quebec City and Montreal; it looks good to say such things. He has just announced another subsidy, but when the minister made that announcement he forgot to say that he was subsidizing everyone who travels on VIA Rail. I do not remember the exact amount, but I think it costs the government about $130 per passenger.

Madam Speaker, I would like to commend Chrysler Canada Ltd. for its recent decision to upgrade its Windsor minivan plant at a total cost of some $600 million. This action speaks volumes about the attractiveness of Canada as an outstanding location for auto sector investment.
This is but one of many new capital investments in Canada announced in the past year by the big three. These investments total over $3.6 billion in value, including $1 billion at the new Ford engine plant in Windsor and $1 billion at its Oakville minivan plant, among others.
These investment announcements clearly indicate that we can compete. Canadian workers are among the world's most productive, second only to the United States and fully six and a half times more productive than their Mexican counterparts.
Ontario is close to major markets in the northeastern United States. Inflation here is lower than in most of the industrialized world and the cost of capital is becoming increasingly competitive. Madam Speaker, sick building syndrome is very real. The Judy LaMarsh Building in Chatham, Ontario, is the regional headquarters for National Health and Welfare. Labour Canada officials closed the building last week and sent its 235 employees home.
Renovations to the sealed building have created problems. Air quality tests found the levels of organic compounds to be up to eight times higher than the acceptable standards. One woman was sent to a hospital
by ambulance with chemical bums to her throat. Fainting and irritated eyes were common.
We must find a cure for these sick buildings. Chatham is just one example. The World Health Organization says 20 per cent of all office buildings and two million workers could be affected. Fumes and lack of proper ventilation are two reasons.
After hearing of the Chatham incident my office has received calls from people in Ottawa and Toronto who have suffered the same situation.
I will be presenting a private member's bill regarding air quality in buildings. We must take action on this issue. It is not just a trendy issue but a serious health issue.

The government has recently instituted a number of programs under Canada's green plan to help address the problems confronting wildlife, its populations and its habitat.

Madam Speaker, the report of the UN truth commission on El Salvador linked 95 per cent of the crimes against humanity during the 12-year civil war to the army. Important recommendations of the commission, such as the removal of the justices of the supreme court and the purging of the 40 military officers named, must be implemented.
The Catholic Church, one of the main negotiators for peace in El Salvador, has paid the supreme price in the civil war with the murder of Archbishop Romero, four American nuns and six Jesuit priests.
Defence Minister General Emilio Ponce and two dozen of his military officers have been directly linked to these murders. Yet within hours of the truth commission's report President Cristiani moved to grant amnesty to all those named, including the release from jail of two of those guilty of murdering the priests.
Canada must press for implementation of the outstanding recommendations of both the truth and ad hoc commissions. Canada must express to President Cristiani, to the UN and all related agencies our absolute outrage with President Cristiani's actions.
The recommendations of the truth commission are obligatory. Every avenue must be explored to prosecute the Salvadoran military officers for atrocities committed during this war.

As a child growing up on the farm in Saskatchewan I looked forward each year to the renewal that spring represented: to the return of the geese from the south, to the birth of the new calves, and to the warming of the soil which meant that the new crop could soon be seeded.
Spring to prairie farmers represents in a real sense the beginning of the new year, and with it comes the eternal optimism for which farmers have been famous for so many years.

Madam Speaker, Windsor retirees and others have been discriminated against in the tax treatment they have received. This issue goes back to 1980 and 1981 when Chrysler workers received shares from the company in return for wage and benefit concessions.
After negotiations in 1985 it was agreed they could cash these shares, but Revenue Canada treated this as income rather than seeing the growth in share values as capital gains.
Under the leadership of the local union president, Larry Bauer, this case went to court. The union won in the end. All active employees who had signed notices of objection received their taxes back plus interest, but over 1,000 retirees and others who had not been able to sign notices received back only their taxes paid. They received no interest.
The Minister of National Revenue has a way to correct this discriminatory treatment under the government's tax fairness package. I strongly urge action.

April 2, 1993

Madam Speaker, I direct my question to the Acting Prime Minister or whoever is speaking for the government today.
I think we are all distressed by reports of the incident in Somalia where four Canadian soldiers are being held in connection with the death of a Somali man. I want to express as well the deep concern that we have about the way in which the matter has been handled and the number of unanswered questions that are still outstanding without any response.
Why did it take so long for the investigation to get under way and for a public accounting on the matter? Why has there been no effort by the minister of defence to present the facts to Parliament? When can we expect the minister of defence to give a full accounting of what has taken place and the situation in which our soldiers are now expected to serve in Somalia?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, under the military legal system it is the responsibility of the commanding officer to immediately begin an investigation into any incident that arises. That occurred immediately.
After a couple of days of local investigation, the commanding officer felt he needed expert assistance from Ottawa. It took a couple of days to get the
passports, inoculations and so on for the experts from Ottawa to proceed to Somalia to carry on the investigation.
There was no delay. The investigation commenced immediately and is ongoing.

Madam Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the same minister.
The problem is about three weeks ago four Canadians were involved in the suspicious death of a Somali. Why did it take so long for the investigation to get under way and why did the Minister of National Defence not state the facts in this case?
I ask the government to report to the House as soon as possible on the circumstances of that tragic incident.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I indicated there was no delay. The investigation commenced immediately. However in the military justice system as in the civilian justice system it is not common practice or the accepted practice, for good and valid reasons which I am sure the hon. member understands, for the investigating officers to conduct, if you will, press conferences on the aspects of the investigation.
There is an investigation taking place. It is confidential, as are all investigations. It would be no more appropriate for the Minister of National Defence to stand in the House and give details than it would be for the Solicitor General to stand in the House and give details on civilian investigations by the RCMP.

Madam Speaker, I am not sure the hon. minister quite understands the implications of what is taking place.
We have close to 5,000 troops involved in 18 complicated, difficult, risky missions around the world. As the minister will remember we have raised questions many times about the lack of any comprehensive approach in our peacekeeping operations, problems of equipment, training and preparation. Instead we have contradictory,
April 2, 1993

piecemeal statements. The Minister of National Defence said this week that we are going to pull the troops out of Bosnia if there is fighting, which there has been for the last two years.
Is it not time for the sake of our troops, families and Canadians that there be a regular system of reporting and accountability on peacekeeping missions so that we know exactly what mandate, what commitment and what circumstances our troops are involved in and to ensure that members of Parliament and the public will not have to learn from the media about tragic incidents such as took place in Somalia but learn, as should be the case, from the minister responsible who should be doing her job?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think the hon. member has two very different subjects confused and he is trying to bring them together. They do not deserve to be brought together.
The question of an alleged criminal act is being investigated quite properly using the well established procedures that have been in place for decades, in fact since this country began.
I think the hon. member would understand that for justice to be done it is necessary for the investigating officers and the authorities to conduct that investigation without the case being prejudiced by comments made in the House.
On the question of our peacekeeping role, surely there is no mystery to the hon. member or anybody else about Canada's willingness and readiness to participate in UN sanctioned peacekeeping roles. The hon. member made a statement that the Minister of National Defence said that if there is fighting we are going to leave Bosnia and there has been fighting for the last year. That is nonsense. She said no such thing.
Yes, she did.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, no. I am sorry. Would the hon. member listen for a moment. She said if our troops are under attack. It is part of the UNPROFOR mandate that if UNPROFOR troops are attacked they will withdraw because our troops are there in Bosnia to try to provide humanitarian aid to the Bosnians. They are not there on a peacekeeping mission. They are there with the UNPROFOR to provide humanitarian aid. If they are
Oral Questions
attacked, they will pull out along with the other UN troops there.
That is what the Minister of National Defence said, not what the hon. member alleged.

Madam Speaker, Canadians and members of Parliament were shocked and disappointed to learn of this incident involving the death of a Somali and four Canadian peacekeepers through the media three weeks after the event.
I want to direct my question to the Acting Prime Minister. As a previous Associate Minister of National Defence he would be aware that the commanding officer is required to send a significant incident report to the Chief of the Defence Staff.
When was the Minister of National Defence briefed on this issue and when does she plan to inform the House? If she was not briefed, why was she not briefed?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member as a former military person would well understand that in the military as in civilian life individuals who may be suspected of having committed a crime are entitled to the normal safety measures, are entitled to be presumed innocent and so on.
In order for investigations to be conducted in a fair manner it is necessary that they be done outside the glare of publicity and done in confidence. That is what is happening.
The Minister of National Defence continues to fulfil her responsibilities as she always has. The question of what her officials have said to her and when they said it, as the hon. member will know, is really not a matter for disclosure on the floor of the House of Commons.

Madam Speaker, the point here is that members of Parliament and Canadians found out through the media.
When did the minister expect that members of Parliament and Canadians should find out? If it was not through the media how were we to find out? It is a significant event. I remind the minister that we have a size and scope of peacekeeping operations unprecedented in Canadian history. We have 4,800 Canadian peacekeepers involved in 18 different locations around the

April 2, 1993
Oral Questions
world. We have 10 per cent of the world peacekeeping operations under way.
Canadians and members of Parliament do not expect, neither should they deserve, to be informed of these incidents in peacekeeping through the media many days and weeks after they have occurred.
I want to ask the Acting Prime Minister if he will appoint a full-time Minister of National Defence who will show leadership in the conduct of these operations and who will implement immediately a formalized regular series of briefings on these operations to the Parliament of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I guess this last question indicates the real interest of the opposition. They are not concerned about justice for the soldiers involved but rather are interested in trying to discredit the Minister of National Defence.
The Minister of National Defence is fulfilling her responsibility in an outstanding manner as she always does with all of her responsibilities. As the hon. member and as all hon. members would know, the appropriate time for comment on an investigation is only after the investigation is complete.

course, Madam Speaker, I predicted that response from the minister so I did not read the rest of my question until I got that response.

areas. He does not believe it and neither do other foreign investors.

speechtext: Does the government have employees in (a) Thunder Bay (b) riding of Thunder Bay-Atikokan (c) riding of Thunder Bay-Nipigon (d) riding of Kenora-Rainy River (e) riding of Cochrane-Superior and, if so, in each case, (i) how many and what is their primary place of employment (ii) are any positions designated as bilingual and, if so, how many and what are their classifications (iii) how many vacancies have occurred in both unilingual and bilingual positions and how many of those have been filled?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
In response to the hon. member's question, the government has 748 Public Service employees in the census metropolitan area of Thunder Bay which includes the ridings of Thunder Bay-Atikokan and Thunder Bay-Nipigon. Of these 748 occupied positions, 27 are bilingual positions. Of these, one is in the scientific and professional categoiy, 13 in administrative and foreign service, one in technical, 11 in administrative support and one in the operational category. There are 721 employees in unilingual positions. Employees are mainly located in the cities of Thunder Bay and Neebing.
There are 377 employees in the riding of Kenora- Rainy River: nine are in bilingual positions, two of which are in the scientific and professional category, four in administrative and foreign service and three in administrative support. There are 368 employees in unilingual positions. Employees are mainly located in Sioux Lookout, Kenora and Fort Frances.
There are 199 employees in the riding of Cochrane-Superior, 21 of whom are in bilingual positions, three in the scientific and professional, eight in administrative support, three in technical and in seven administrative support. There are 178 employees in unilingual positions. The majority of the employees are located in Hearst, Kapuskasing, and in the census subdivision of Cochrane, unorganized north part.
In the 1992 Public Service recruitment in Ontario excluding Toronto and the national capital region, of 1,425 new recruits, 1,328 or 93 per cent were appointed to unilingual positions and 97 were appointed to bilingual positions.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to indicate that we are prepared to support the amendment that is moved by the hon. member.
We were happy with the bill as it stands. The amendment makes some sense, however, since registration as a party is a significant act. We are quite prepared to support the position he puts forward that 1,000 electors ought to sign the party's application for registration. The geographical distribution makes some sense. We are happy to support the amendment.

Madam Speaker, I must say that my whole purpose today at report stage, as I unfortunately was not here during the debate on second reading, is to focus some attention on the plight and problems of Independent members.
This is obviously for registered parties. I congratulate the Lortie commission. I know the committee of parliamentarians has worked hard on producing this phase of the electoral reform. I was just informed by the government House leader that the second phase, which definitely has some more areas of very real critical interest, may be coming and perhaps will be a priority once we come back from the Easter break. It is really the reverse side of this amendment. I do not really have any problem with this amendment because it concerns registered parties.
I have a real problem with several sections in the present bill that are silent about the status of Independent members. The fundamental one is the inability of Independent members to give tax receipts. Members of a registered party, be they Conservative, Liberal or NDP, can and that is understandable. However members of the Green Party, the Rhinoceros Party or parties that had 50 candidates in the last election can get a receipt.
Sitting members in this House who have stated they are Independents and are going to run in the next election are not able to get a receipt before the writ is issued. This puts that Independent candidate in a very unfavourable situation against candidates who are members of registered parties.
I understand the need for registered parties. I belonged to a registered party for years. For certain reasons, which we will not repeat here, I am no longer a member of a registered party but am quite happy to be here as an Independent.
The only two negatives to that situation are getting recognized by the Chair, but I will leave that aside, and with regard to elections Independents cannot give a tax receipt as their competitors can. That puts Independents in an unfair disadvantage.
The government House leader just told me this is going to be corrected in phase two. I have been following this debate with interest. I have correspondence with the government House leader going back to 1991 on this problem, which he recognizes and the Lortie commission recognized.
I give full credit to the Lortie commission. I presented a brief before the Lortie commission and its chairman, Pierre Lortie, an eminent Canadian. He and the interesting group on his commission produced an $18 million to $20 million report that produced a wealth of changes. I am sorry that we are not going to change many more things.
I know the wish of the government and the Chief Electoral Officer has indicated to the committee that he wants this phase passed so that forward planning can be done and implemented in time for the next election. We all know that is going to come some time between now and the early fall, September or October at the latest. We are hoping to use the referendum list. Surely the government would not call an election and not utilize the referendum list that cost $125 million to produce.
We know there is going to be an election. I do not want to impede the work of the Chief Electoral Officer, Mr. Kingsley, who has taken over from that other great Canadian, Jean-Marc Hamel, who came into this scene as the Chief Electoral Officer almost at the time I did some 25 years ago.
I do find it difficult being co-operative this afternoon when I know the government and the committee have looked after the problems of lunatics and have looked after the problems of prisoners voting in jails, perhaps not very well, but they have not looked after the problem I have raised.
April 2, 1993

Government Orders
I wish I could get some assurance from the government House leader and that might change my obstinance at the moment because I understand the reason and I do not want to be difficult. Someone could say that people who are Independents must be lunatics. I suppose that might be the answer of my colleague, the government House leader. I said someone might say that. J'aifait une blague, une petite blague.
I would like some assurance on this question because I have some problems with extending the vote to lunatics. This problem affecting Independents has been well known by the government House leader for three years. It was described in the Lortie commission which provided a remedy and in the draft bill set up a draft wording that could be used.
I am very disappointed that the committee did not recommend and the government House leader in the introduction of Bill C-114 has not dealt with the problem in this phase so that an Independent member could start to issue receipts just like some of the people he will be running against who are issuing them today.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to put on the record what I said to the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants privately. It is the intention of the government to proceed with phase two of electoral reform.
The reason for this is that the committee, in looking at this electoral reform in the Lortie report, concluded that because it was such a big mouthful it would be expeditious to proceed with those things that impose on the Chief Electoral Officer a large administrative burden such as these special ballots.
We decided to do that in one phase and we had thought we would have it through the House by now. The second phase would deal with the whole question of financing, limits, eligible expenses and the question of the private member's ability to write tax receipts.
I am told and assured, and I would be very disappointed if it was not there and I am sure it is there, that the report of the committee will include the amendments to the act to make it possible for private members to bring forward the bill.
If the hon. member wants further assurances why this would be something the government would be most interested in, he well knows that the existing limits and rules pertaining to fund raising are grossly inadequate. All of us are under pressure, so to speak, from our parties to amend the act in that regard. Therefore it is very much a government priority.

Madam Speaker, I was listening to the leader of the government talk about pressures from the three political parties represented in this House to amend the Canada Elections Act. We in the Bloc Quebecois, and of course the independent members of this House, should also be included in there.
We must debate amendments but, as the leader of the ruling party said earlier, we would have liked to deal with the whole issue of amending the elections act. We are dealing with the first phase today, when elections are to be called by next October at the latest. Between now and then we will not have the time to look at phase two which deals with political party financing.
This amendment makes it totally impossible for an independent candidate to run except under very specific circumstances. I think that is totally unfair. It is unfair from a democratic point of view in the sense that only pre-registered parties seem to be recognized. Bear in mind that there are always people in an election who want to use a platform to promote their own views.
Obviously a ruling party can with legislation like that limit debate. As a matter of fact this government has done it and the fact was recognized again through parliamentary procedure. Time allocation can be used now pretty well as government pleases. Debate can even be stalled by the presentation of motions. Just about anything goes now.
In our opinion the amendment put forward by my colleague is perfectly justifiable. However it is restrictive, and that concerns us greatly. It is impossible to deal with this specific amendment in isolation from the bill as a whole, a bill which is being tabled in stages in spite of the fact that the Official Opposition had demanded, at the time this first phase was tabled, that it be provided

April 2, 1993
Government Orders
with the complete picture not only the parts that suited the government first and the opposition second.
On the other hand, not all the amendments before us today come from the Official Opposition. There are also some from the New Democratic Party. Had we been invited to discuss the matter-which was virtually settled right there and then-with the traditional and recognized parties represented in this House we could have made an important contribution.
In that context I do not believe we can agree to pass in a great rush amendments to such an important bill for democracy but at the same time this bill must take into account the significant issue of political party financing.
In this connection, we all know that big multinational companies routinely make contributions to the traditional parties and that these contributions can reach hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Last night on TV, we saw the multinationals that contributed to the yes committee fund for the referendum held last October. The same thing could happen again in the next election because we will not have dealt with phase two. There will be restrictions, however, on independent candidates who will not be able to seek funding and give tax receipts because there is no provision in the legislation. A party must field at least 50 candidates to be officially recognized by the Chief Electoral Officer. As a result, the democratic principle of this bill is being truncated. It is really too bad just before the Easter holidays when members will go back to their ridings to do the job that we have to do. We are being told today that if it does not pass now the Canada Elections Act will not be amended in time for the next election, which is practically a threat.
However, if we do accept these amendments, if we do accept this phase of electoral reform, we are accepting changes that suit the traditional parties in a House that some people see as a private club. I think that is unfortunate and undemocratic.
In my own case if I decided to run as an independent in the next election campaign, I would not be able to give tax receipts to people who would like to contribute to my
campaign fund. This introduces a bias in our democratic system. The traditional parties are recognized. They can accept any amount they wish. They can give tax receipts to people and companies but an independent candidate would not be able to do that.
It is unfortunate and, as I see it, practically an insult to our democratic system that we do not have all the amendments to the Canada Elections Act but only those amendments that suit the interests of the government and the Official Opposition. That being the case, we in the Bloc Quebecois are firmly opposed to the passage of Bill C-114 because this legislation totally ignores democratic principles and the democratic rights of potential candidates in the next election campaign.
In fact the amendment moved by the hon. member would be most welcome as part of a bill that would cover all phases. However, we are amending the Canada Elections Act in instalments. The first instalment is very convenient for the government because it minimizes the chances of having independent candidates and submits them to restrictions imposed by this Parliament.
That being the case, we will do our best to explain to this government the importance of these amendments, whether they are adopted today or tomorrow, but of course tomorrow the House will be closed, since we are supposed to adjourn today.
It never fails. At the end of the session we are always pressured to adopt a number of important bills, practically without warning. They want to rush this through and one, two, three, these are the bills you have to pass. We have to accommodate the government and we have to accommodate the Official Opposition. The New Democratic Party has a number of amendments and the Liberal Party has several as well, but when I see this organized attempt to push through a bill I think this contravenes the basic principles of democracy and we will not go along with this.

Madam Speaker, I will discuss the amendments tabled today in the report of the electoral reform committee. When this reform got underway with the Lortie commission, people were asked to send briefs and I did submit a rather short one on the financing of political parties.
April 2, 1993

I will admit that I was totally disappointed to see that the issue of financing will not be discussed before the next election campaign. When you look at the way political parties are financed you wonder if we live in a true democracy. In Quebec we made very important changes to the elections act regarding party financing. All companies, multinationals, law firms, engineering firms, et cetera, were prohibited from making contributions so that only a voter could make a gift to a political party.
In Quebec the limit was set at $3,000. I thought it was high but I never understood why.
In my brief to the commission on electoral reform I wrote that in a democracy the financing of political parties was something extremely important and that it is up to the public to ensure that all those who want to run for a seat in this House have an equal chance to do so. No company and no wealthy individual should have the right to make unlimited contributions to help elect a party or a candidate.
Studies have been made on this. A University of New Brunswick professor gathered data for several years. I read his doctoral thesis at that institution. This person had asked me if I could provide information. Indeed, with the help of the Library of Parliament and with questions taken from the Order Paper, I was able to provide the required information.
This information proved extremely important. Each year when people make donations to a political party they get a receipt and they are entitled to a tax credit. The administration of this system represents several million dollars.
This professor's approach, which I found to be very good, is simply that if we believe in a democratic system and if we truly want to make our system equal and fair, we should eliminate all contributions to political parties. It is up to the public, to the community to ensure that those men and women who want to be candidates have funds at their disposal.
This professor demonstrated that to set up such a system would only cost 99 cents per voter. It would only cost 99 cents per voter to ensure that we have the most democratic system, as well as the fairest.
Government Orders
The total amount, which would be around $26 or $27 million, would be distributed to political parties. There would be a very fair system for the splitting of that money. No company, nor any voter, even the wealthiest ones, would be allowed to make a contribution. The state would make sure that anyone who is a candidate gets enough money to campaign. Then lobbyists would not be able to influence politicians. No company, no individual should have the right to influence the decisions of this House. This is not normal. The only way to put an end to it is to make sure that no one-no group, no union, no company, no engineering firm, no law firm-has the right to exert pressure on an individual who is a candidate by telling him: We are going to finance your campaign. We are going to contribute significantly to your election. In a just and equitable system this should be illegal.
This aspect has been totally ignored. I respect the work of the commission and the efforts which were made. There were probably things to be amended but doing nothing with regard to this vital aspect, the financing of political parties, is inexcusable. Several amendments to the bill will be proposed today. We talked about it at length but we never did anything about the real problem, the financing of political parties. In my opinion the way things stand we are open to corruption. That is for sure. Proposing formulas and holding discussions is simply beating around the bush.
To conclude, I believe that with time it will come. It is inescapable. As people become more concerned, more politicized, they realize that it does not make sense to leave financing of political parties to the well-to-do of this country.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am also pleased to rise to participate in the debate on such a controversial and questionable bill which is a mini reform of the elections act when we were expecting a full reform of the legislation.
I would like to quote what the right hon. Prime Minister had to say, 15 days before the last election, and what made the front page of La Presse. I would like the government House leader to listen instead of talking with his neighbour as he is doing right now. Here is a quote from that article: "Mr. Mulroney wants parties to be financed by the general public". That is a firm

April 2, 1993
Government Orders
commitment he made ten days before the last election, on November 17 to be exact, which was actually only five days before the election. He made that commitment and said to the reporter: "It is important to act now since it would be unfair to change the rules just a few weeks or a month before an election compaign. That is why we will deal with this issue early on during our mandate". Then-mandate is almost over and at the very last minute, contrary to the official commitment made by the Prime Minister five days before an election, they come up with a mini reform which restricts democracy in Canada and, as indirectly, in Quebec.
How can they restrict, with the amendment mentioned earlier, the very first amendment before the House? We are being told that 1,000 voters from at least 50 different districts will have to sign an application and submit it to Elections Canada. An individual who wants to bring together residents from one area to elect a member supporting their regional interests would be disqualified almost automatically. If he lives in Vancouver can he afford to go to 50 ridings and all the way to Ontario to find one person, one qualified voter, to sign the application? Can he afford to go all over the country to gather 1,000 signatures in order to be recognized?
With this amendment what treatment would the independent members sitting next to me get? What treatment would the green party on the environment get? What treatment would the social credit party get, which still exists in some areas of Quebec and western Canada? What treatment would those parties get which, for example, want to promote or oppose free trade, abortion or the right to life? What treatment would those who want to form a political party get?
This amendment would severely restrict these groups and thus would also hinder the democratic process. In fact this amendment only serves the interest of the three main political parties in this House.
This amendment creates a sort of preserve and I cannot accept the fact that no Conservative member from Quebec wants to talk on this issue. After all, these members are aware of the historic legacy left by Rene Levesque who in 1977, after he became prime minister of our province, had as one of his priorities the democratization of political parties through financing by the
people. Only those who have the right to vote have the right to finance political parties in Quebec.
Following this display of courage the right hon. Prime Minister had committed himself, five days before the election, to table a bill in the first few months of his term. Instead he waited until the last minute to introduce a bill which would again protect the interests of those who finance his political party, namely the big multinationals which give $100,000 or $200,000 to his party in an attempt to buy the popular vote and ensure the survival of the party.
As for the other parties, I was surprised and pleased to hear the previous speaker, the member for Gatineau, who discussed the financial aspect of this issue and who would also like to see an in-depth review of this financing which should be the intent of the legislation.
When the government talks about electoral reform it must first discuss financing. It overlooked that aspect during the last referendum by saying the same thing. According to Mr. Justice Michaud the legislation on the financing of the last referendum was anti-democratic. Mr. Justice Michaud said that it was a violation of democracy not to impose a limit to the parties involved in a referendum or an election when it comes to approaching various organizations and collecting money from them.
Mr. Justice Michaud was very clear on this. The government invoked the Charter of Rights and Freedoms as the reason not to limit the financial involvement of people or corporations. In his decision Mr. Justice Michaud said this: "It is much more harmful to let the multinationals finance at large, as much as they want, the political parties or the yes or no side during the referendum". It is much more dangerous for democracy than to limit those contributions because the "democratic process must not be influenced by money or advertising." This is what Mr. Justice Michaud wrote in the Libman decision: "It must not be influenced by an avalanche of advertising, a slew of commercial messages which could have the effect of jeopardizing the democratic process".
The Liberals and the New Democrats are accomplices of the Conservative Party in this debate by accepting such a minor reform which will nevertheless impose
April 2, 1993

rather serious restrictions, especially for small political parties.
Mr. Vezina who phoned me from Toronto told me: "This reform-"
Someone is knocking at the door, Madam Speaker.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we were still debating Motion No. 2 restricting the right of political parties to be bom, thereby limiting the right to exercise democracy in Canada and in Quebec. It calls for one thousand electors from 50 different electoral districts. It may be warranted in some cases to limit the number of people who would want to register as members of a political party, but I think that such limitation goes completely against the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It takes us back once more to this ongoing problem in the history of our democracy, namely the power of the wealthy relative to the rest of the population.
Unavoidably when established parties like the Progressive Conservative Party, the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party get together and agree to limit our right to exercise democracy they are protecting their

April 2, 1993
Government Orders
ivoiy tower at the expense of democracy. In that context I can only oppose such a legislation.
Again the real problem requiring an in-depth revision of the elections act is political party financing. That particular question has been evaded, although the Lortie commission did mention it in its report without being too demanding. The hon. member for Megan tic-Compton-Stanstead did request it in a report submitted to the Lortie commission but it was disregarded. They did not even take into account in that reform the Prime Minister's firm commitment to ensure that the financing would come from the public at large, which means that only those who have the right to vote could contribute. We must fiercely protect that heritage from the days when Rene Levesque was premier of Quebec. I cannot understand that the conservative members of this House do not care enough for this legacy to allow us to vote democratically without being influenced by money.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, thank you for giving me this opportunity this afternoon to speak on Bill C-114 which in no way reflects the promise of the Conservative Party for a thorough reform, particularly in the area of party financing.
I would like to quote the promise of the Prime Minister, just before the election, to bring financing of political parties by the general public. We can find it in La Presse dated November 17, 1988, and I quote: "A bill to force all political parties at the federal level to rely on financing by the general public would be passed at the very beginning of the second mandate of a Conservative government". This was the assurance given by Prime Minister Brian Mulroney during an exclusive interview to the Montreal daily La Presse.
Such a measure would be a logical and fundamental initiative to eradicate a number of potential conflicts of interest. That is what the Prime Minister was saying just before the election of 1988 with a view, naturally, of securing votes in Quebec because he knew that this mode of financing had now existed for a number of years in Quebec. It is now part of Quebec culture.
Being well aware that it was in the Quebec culture he used it just before the election of 1988 in order to win votes.
I continue my quote: "Recognizing without reservations the value of such a measure already in existence in Quebec, Mr. Mulroney said he would legislate quickly an end to contributions by corporate entities, whether companies or unions, to election funds of political parties, and a limitation to contributions by individuals. He said he would put all his weight in the balance to convince reluctant members of his own party before proceeding as quickly as possible with such a legislation.
For the outgoing Prime Minister, such a legislation on financing by the general public would fit his commitment of openness already shown by new and stricter regulations regarding conflicts of interest and an act on registration of lobbyists.
It is precisely his approach to problems of the past which, according to him, convinced Canadian voters of his commitment and of the need to minimize risks by taking the necessary measures to deal with the source of the most common errors and, among those measures, he is greatly relying on the financing of political parties by the people".
This is a formal statement made by a Prime Minister who seemed credible at the time and who got my trust. I belonged then to his party and he was then my leader. I believed in this Prime Minister and his statements, such as the one I just mentioned to you.
Moreover, the leader of the Bloc Quebecois, who was at the time his Quebec lieutenant, believed as well in the Prime Minister and in his statements on financing by individuals. He firmly believed in that. Indeed, he was one of the few in his riding of Lac-Saint-Jean to adopt, as an example, the financing by individuals for the 1988 election.
Another member from the Bloc Quebecois, the hon. member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead, was the one, and everybody in this House knows it and I know that most Quebecers also know it, who defended financing by the people in order to avoid conflicts of interest.

As usual the Prime Minister in order to cover up his intentions as he did with several other projects or initiatives opposed by Quebecers or Canadians or to improve some sectors of economic or political activities because he wants to wash his hands of the issue, always ends up appointing boards of inquiry which cost millions of dollars to the Crown and to the taxpayers. It costs millions and millions of dollars. Besides the Prime Minister to gain time said that he wanted to do it at the very beginning of his next mandate. But to wash his hands of the matter he simply appointed a commission which was called the Lortie commission. This Lortie commission cost a few million dollars.
It made many recommendations, particularly one on financing by the general public as the Prime Minister had asked it to do. It did not have any choice because the Prime Minister had publicly requested that. It being the case inevitably, Mr. Lortie, who was the chairman of this commission, had to comply with that request. Now we have Bill C-114, but unfortunately the part which seemed to have priority for the Prime Minister is not in it. It was completely left aside and here we are trying to deal with a few small amendments, though important indeed, which do not solve the basic problem which is the financing of political parties.
The referendum is not that far behind us. It was held last fall, in October. The Canada Elections Act was used to establish the rules for that October 1992 referendum. Just last night, on CBC if I am not mistaken, expenses for that referendum were made public. "correctional institution as a result of a conviction and has been sentenced to five or more years in a correctional institution;".
He said: Madam Speaker, these two motions are really alternative motions. I have brought these amendments to this bill to allow the House the opportunity to express its views on whether or not inmates should be granted the right to vote.
As we no doubt are aware under the current law prisoners are denied the right to vote in the written part of section 51 of the Canada Elections Act. The words of the act that are relevant are:
The following persons are not qualified to vote at an election and
shall not vote at an election:
(e) Every person undergoing punishment as an inmate in any penal institution for the commission of any offence.
There is a blanket ban under the current law on any inmate exercising the right to vote. That section of the Canada Elections Act was declared null and void by the courts under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The charter guarantees every citizen the right to vote and that right was taken away by this section of the Canada Elections Act. The courts concluded that imprisonment alone was not sufficient justification for striking down the right to vote and accordingly it struck down the section of the Canada Elections Act thereby restoring the right to vote to inmates in institutions.
During the referendum campaign that was just concluded, the right to vote was extended to inmates. In fact there was no civil insurrection or great problem because inmates exercised their franchise during the referendum
campaign.
Inmates in institutions were able to vote only in the place where they actually resided, that is where their families reside or from where they had been sentenced. Residence in the institution in and of itself did not constitute residence for the purpose of determining where an inmate voted. Although there is a very large prison population, for example in Kingston and the Islands, only something like 119 inmates registered to vote in Kingston and the Islands.
In addition, inmates must apply to register. Many did not. Something like one-third of the inmates in Canada chose to register in the referendum. While it could be expected that more might register in the case of a general election, under the rules that were proposed they would vote only in the place where they live and not in the prison where they are residing at the time of their imprisonment.
The government established the Royal Commission on Electoral Reform and Party Financing which made a recommendation in respect of inmates voting. It recommended a double-barrelled test. It recommended that those serving a life sentence with a minimum of 10 or more years to be served not be allowed to vote, but all other inmates be granted the right to vote. The committee which was studying the report, of which I was a member, concluded that test was too broad or unsatisfactory in one way or another and came up with a slightly more detailed proposal which I will not go into. The government, when it received the committee report, rejected out of hand all the committee's recommendations. It came up with a proposal in Bill C-114 which denied the right to vote to every person who is imprisoned in a correctional institution serving a sentence of two years or more.
That disenfranchises every single inmate in a federal institution in Canada since in order to be sentenced to a federal prison inmates have to receive a sentence of two years or more. All other offenders who receive a lesser sentence spend their time in a provincial jail.
In the circumstances I feel this is harsh and unfair. Therefore I have proposed two amendments which were read to the House. The first would extend the right to vote to all inmates; the second would extend it to all inmates serving a sentence of five years or less. If they got five years or more then they would have no right to vote.
The five-year rule is designed to appeal to perhaps a wider segment of members in the House than the blanket lifting of the restriction would otherwise do. I suspect the first one might get defeated on a vote in the House; the second I would hope the government would see fit to support. Clearly if it does not, the motion is going to go down too.
I want to say something about my reason for proposing these amendments. The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which is paramount in our legal structure and which creates certain rights for all citizens, does give the right to all citizens to vote. By sentencing a person to prison it is not the intent of the judge in imposing the sentence or indeed of the criminal law under which the sentence is rendered, to take away from that inmate his or her right of citizenship. Clearly it is a kind of punishment. That is why an inmate is sentenced to prison. It is not because the prisoner or accused person is being stripped of his or her citizenship.
If inmates in prisons are citizens and if we accept that our charter is the highest law in our country, then surely it follows that inmates in prison who are citizens ought to have the right to vote just as everyone else does. It does
April 2, 1993

not aid in the punishment that the person not have a right to vote.
I guess I would have to issue a challenge to the government to say how it is that by sentencing someone to prison we punish the person further by taking away the right to vote. It is a right that is a free right given in a democratic society. It is freely given in our society. While it may satisfy some innate sense of justice in some of us to think that prisoners ought to be deprived of the right to vote, it serves no useful purpose either in punishing the inmate or in the rehabilitation of the inmate, which after all is part of the aim of the imprisonment process.
We sentence inmates to a jail term in the hope that at the conclusion of the sentence they will be able to come out and establish themselves in a normal and law abiding way in the community. We do not sentence them to prison with the idea that when they come out they will be committing more crimes and sent back. That is not the aim. Sometimes it happens, I agree, but it is not the aim.
Surely if that is not the aim we ought to be careful to ensure that the steps taken in respect of a prisoner in terms of denial of rights and denial of responsibilities ought to be commensurate with the sentence. While it is easy to say that a sentence of two years or more justifies certain action, like being placed in a federal penitentiary, does it really help the case to then say in addition they are not going to be allowed to vote? Frankly I expect most inmates could not care less, but as a democratic society based on the rule of law, which has as its guiding principle the notion that every citizen has the right to vote, surely we should be thinking very hard before we deprive certain citizens of that right.
The purpose of these amendments is to ensure that the right is restored in a reasonable and sensible way and not in a way that allows mass voting of inmates in the places in which they are resident; that is in prisons. The voting will take place in prisons, but the votes will be cast in the constituency in which the inmate resided or in which his family resides at the time the vote is to be cast. I think that is a fair way of doing it.
Government Orders
I should point out that the system I have suggested in Motion No. 3, whereby all inmates would have the right to vote, is one that is followed in Italy, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Ireland and Israel. In our own country in the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland, inmates in institutions have the right to vote. Some of the provinces have gone far beyond what the government is proposing in Bill C-114.
I urge the government to consider adopting either Motion No. 3 or Motion No. 4 in amendment to this bill in order to widen the franchise and give the right to vote where it has been taken away, in my view unnecessarily and possibly unfairly.

House leader. This is the electoral reform bill that affects all members and actually affects all people who are going to vote. It is really a fairly important piece of legislation.

the Receiver General and not just go back to the Consolidated Revenue Fund.

they Liberal, Conservative, NDP, Rhinoceros, Green or Bloc Quebecois.
