Madam Speaker, I would like to say a few things on these motions that talk about the right to vote for those in federal penal institutions.
The member for Kingston and the Islands who has proposed the amendments has taken us through some of the history of what the Supreme Court did to section 51 of the present elections act. He also reviewed what the electoral commission recommended, that those with a prison term of more than 10 years would be denied the right to vote.
This bill recommends two years. That means that everyone in a federal penal institution would lose the right to vote. The motion tries to strike a balance, half way between what this bill is recommending and the 10 years. Therefore, put it at five years.
I would like to say something about the arguments that the member used. He used primarily two arguments. The member stressed the fact that the Charter of Rights and Freedoms says that all citizens have the right to vote. That is correct.
The member went on to say that people imprisoned in a federal institution do not lose their citizenship. That is correct. However, they do lose other rights that are in the charter. They lose the obvious right to mobility which is in the charter. They cannot move around. They cannot take up residence. They have to stay in that prison. Therefore, they have lost that right.
They also lose the right to freedom or liberty which all the rest of the citizens of Canada have. That person is deprived of the right to liberty and is now locked up for a

Government Orders
period of time in prison. Therefore they lose other rights.
The member is saying that since they do not lose their citizenship, why are we taking away the right to vote? He is ignoring the fact that they lose the right to mobility, to liberty and other things.
The second reason why prisoners should have the right to vote is that some provinces give people in provincial penal institutions the right to vote. Some other countries do as well.
Some other countries do some weird and wonderful things. Just because they do them does not mean we have to copy them. In fact I am glad we do not copy everything that all other countries do. Therefore, that is not a good argument.
Some provinces do some things. I am glad that we do not copy everything that the socialist republic of Ontario is doing. The same is true for Saskatchewan and British Columbia. Just because some provinces do some things does not mean we should do them.
I fail to see what the arguments are. I would submit that when a person commits a crime, is convicted and is then sentenced into a federal penal institution, which means more than two years, they should lose their right to vote. Common sense would dictate that.
Is it not common sense to say: Now you have lost the normal democratic rights of liberty, mobility and freedom to vote. Until you have served that time and are out of prison, you lose those rights. One of those privileges is the right to vote.
The argument in favour of what the government is saying as to why everyone in a federal penal institution should lose their right to vote is simple common sense. They chose to act against society. They now suffer the consequences which means denial of freedom. One of the aspects of denial of freedom, to move around and be at liberty is they have lost the right to vote.
Simple common sense tells us they have lost the privileges of free, responsible citizens for a fixed period of time. One of those privileges is the right to vote. Therefore I am glad to support what the government is saying, that a person in a federal penal institution should
not have the right to vote. I think that simple common sense tells us that is the right way to go.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to take part in the debate on Motions Nos. 3 and 4. First of all, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands for proposing these amendments. He seems to be more in touch with reality than the Conservative member who spoke to these amendments.
The Conservative member said that a person who commits a crime and is sentenced to a prison term of more than two years should lose all his or her democratic rights, including the right to vote. He must be very unhappy to sit on the Conservative side since several of his colleagues may soon lose that right.
Let us talk about the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Does it limit the right of a person to vote because of something that he or she may have done at some point in his or her life? For example, an inmate in an isolated moment of violence may have committed a crime. An inmate at some point in his life when he was young-we know that some leadership candidates admit to smoking drugs in their early years-Had they been caught then they would have been liable to a three-year jail sentence. In 1970, some people were sentenced to three years in prison just for possession of marijuana. Today those leadership hopefuls say that what they did is insignificant, that it belongs to the past and that it is not serious, and I admit that it is not serious, but it was considered serious then. Some people went to jail for that in those days. What would have happened if those candidates to the leadership of the Conservative Party had been caught and sentenced to three years in jail? They would have lost their right to vote during that period.
These leadership candidates would have lost their right to vote because they would have been sentenced or imprisoned. That is common sense.
The charter of rights is not there to pass judgment on people. It is there to protect their historic rights to live in a democratic society and to assert even more their rights to live in a democracy. To live in democracy one has to be able to elect members of Parliament by voting for the candidate of his or her choice. That is what democracy is all about, to be able to cast a vote every four or five years

at the municipal, provincial or federal levels. speakerposition: Bloc Québécois Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands for the amendment he moved to this most undemocratic bill, a bill that limits the freedom of speech, particularly for prisoners.
It is completely unacceptable to deprive of the right to vote inmates who have been sentenced to more than two years in prison. Taking this right away from a group of citizens reflects an excessive conservatism or liberalism. The main freedom we can have in a country such as ours is the opportunity to decide every four to five years how our country is to be run and how we are going to secure a better quality of life.
Obviously punishment has already been meted out to prisoners but they will be free again some day. They have to keep exercising their rights since most of them will not
be in prison for the rest of their life. They need their freedom of speech because when they come out of prison they will have to live in a society that will have changed. Without the right to vote they may not want to be part of a society which has changed so much.
It seems to me that someone should have the right to vote even if he was sentenced to more than two years in prison because, and I say it again, it is strictly what society wants, the right to express oneself and to change some rules in a country where we advocate the well-being of people.
There is another reason I agree with the proposal. One day that prisoner will get out of prison. I know it because I have a halfway house in my riding. A prisoner who gets out of prison can go to that house in order to re-leam how to live in society. A prisoner who spent 10, 15 or 20 years in prison is totally out of touch with the reality of life when he gets out.
The hon. member for Gaspe, who is a psychologist, should understand very well the difficulties of a prisoner who enters that new life, after spending 10 or 15 years in prison.
In Longueuil, we have a halfway house. Once in a while an ex-prisoner comes and tells me how difficult it is to be back in the real world, how difficult it is to deal with financial institutions, to learn about all the changes in society. Nowadays a generation is only five years. It used to be 10 or 15 years. To call it a new generation there has to be enough changes and now it happens after five years. Our society is changing so fast that if one is away for five years reintegration is difficult. That is the reason why rehabilitation of former inmates is so difficult even after just five years.
I say that inmates should have the right to vote because such a right would keep them in contact with society, would keep them interested. They can then listen to what is going on outside, especially in politics. They can feel that they are still somehow part of society. The day they come out may be sooner than they expected, thanks to our parole system. Rehabilitation might be faster.
April 2, 1993

I think that is a very good reason to support this proposal giving inmates the right to vote.
There is no doubt that if you consider that uncaringly, without a broad perspective, the way the Conservative member did a moment ago-and he is a real Conservative, very shortsighted-then you think that the inmate has been sentenced and must be punished. I agree that he has to be punished if he committed a crime or if he is a threat to society. At the same time we have to recognize that the inmate has the right to remain in touch with society. Otherwise, the day he comes out he will be lost and if he cannot find an answer to his problems in this society he will become a repeat offender.
The other important point is that this person will probably be caught committing a subsequent offence because he will find no other way of adapting to that society. We all know what the costs of prisoner rehabilitation are for government. It is very expensive, but it is also socially disturbing because these people have difficulty fitting in and they risk, as I mentioned before, going astray again and being sent back to prison.
In such a case, you know what the costs are. I was told it costs approximately $60,000 a year to keep an inmate in prison. Therefore, think about the cost of a second offender, the transition cost for someone who gave up on society. You must take into account the fact that this amendment, which gives a prisoner the right to vote, will also allow that individual, on the one hand, to keep in touch with society, to stay interested in what is going on, and on the other hand, to exercise his freedom of speech. For example if human rights are threatened inside the prison he will have the opportunity to express himself freely on that matter if he has the right to vote. That is why I feel it is important that this amendment be passed for all the reasons I just mentioned.

This is so undignified for a government member to prevent an opposition member from speaking his mind. We had to form a political party and come here to defend Quebec's higher interests. And those interests are telling me I should say yes, the prisoners should have the right to vote; they are telling me I should say no one can limit the number of political parties nor limit or control democracy with money, as Justice Michaud said in his decision on the Libman case, nor limit the right for members of other assemblies to become candidates. Let's take an example. There are, in certain provinces like Ontario and Quebec, members of the provincial assembly. They play a role as important as that of the federal members of Parliament. But in smaller provinces, Prince Edward Island for example, where there are 32 MLAs for a territory and a population the size of my riding, evidently the four federal members have much more visibility.
Of course, they have much more visibility. And we should let those people who sit in a provincial legislature be candidates in a federal election without having to resign. That in the opinion of this House, the government should make the Declaration and Plan of Action of the World Summit for Children, held at the United Nations on the 29th and 30th of September, 1990, an integral part of Canadian international co-operation policy;
That the government should consider fully implementing the major global commitments agreed to by the 71 heads of state and government attending the summit, including domestic and international co-operation strategies for child survival and development;
That the government should consider making available adequate financial resources for these purposes, including a contribution to the additional resources required from donor countries based on Canada's historical 5 per cent share of global foreign aid;
That multinational institutions be directed to focus their efforts on the implementation of summit promises;
That the minister responsible for the summit follow-up be invited to report to Parliament once a year on the implementation of the World Summit for Children Plan of Action and the Convention on the Rights of the Child to the extent that the application of the plan and convention, at the national, regional and international levels, requires action or a contribution on the part of Canada; and
That parliamentarians around the world be invited to ensure that each country provide its fair share of the additional resources required to see that the promises of the World Summit for Children become reality.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as you and others may have noticed, Motion No. 616 is almost identical to one that was passed in this House in mid-December 1991. It had the support of all parties in the House.
The fact that these are almost the same is not a coincidence. This motion was presented to the House on November 7, 1991 in an attempt to push the government into some action on the commitments that Canada had made at the World Summit for Children.
More than one year earlier in September 1990, this House passed a motion such as the one we are debating today after waiting the year. Now two and one half years after the world summit, because this government has not
fulfilled its commitment, we are again pushing the government for action.
The 1990 summit for children was the largest gathering of world leaders in history at the time. Prime ministers, presidents and kings promised two billion children a revolution. The Prime Minister was the summit's co-chairman and he invited children everywhere to "listen carefully to what we say and in coming years hold us to our commitments".
I am here today to remind the government that it has not yet fulfilled those commitments. The commitment that Canada and the 58 other countries represented at the summit made was that children would have first call on their government's resources.
Now, two and a half years later, the Prime Minister's noble words and global commitment to reduce child death and malnutrition, to reduce the number of women dying during pregnancy and to make life for all children of the world easier now ring hollow. These words have had little impact on the real world of children today.
In fact, if we are to judge Canada's efforts by the dwindling dollars spent on humanitarian aid Canada has been backing away from those commitments made over and over by this government.
The children of Canada, the children of the world, have found that you cannot depend upon this government to keep its word. Promises cannot be eaten or turned into health care.
By December 1991, 71 countries had agreed to a plan of action in a convention on the rights of the child. Canada joined that group and again committed itself to a massive move to improve the life of children.
This subject of care of children can be dealt with in two parts: domestically for the children here in Canada who have not done particularly well, and internationally for the children of the rest of the world. Canada's record is not great at either level.
I want to spend my short time dealing with the international situation. Many of my colleagues have taken other opportunities to document Canada's lack of commitment to our own children. I want to deal with our
April 2, 1993

commitment to alleviating poverty and reducing the deaths of children from malnutrition and disease all over the world.
In 1992, UNICEF estimated that 40,000 children die every day from infection and malnutrition. That amounts to about 14 million children per year who die because of disease and malnutrition.
I do not want to leave the impression that Canada has not been generous or compassionate. Among the nations of the world Canada has always been among the first to provide emergency food and disaster relief when it has been asked for. Canada also has been and continues to be generous in its donations to multinational organizations such as UNICEF, the children's fund, to UNDP, the development program, and UNIFEM, the UNDP women's program, and to other multinational organizations.
My concern is that we seem to be backing away from our commitment to children, away from the alleviation of poverty in the poorest countries of the world and from the real commitment we made when we signed the Convention on the Rights of the Child in December 1991.
We are backing away from the commitments we made when we accepted sharing our future as the policy base for Canadian aid. That policy was to a great extent a product of three different parliamentary committees in this House.
Proof that Canada is backing away from its commitments is best indicated by the following facts. Canada's aid as a percentage of gross national product is now lower than it has been since the early 1980s. It has fallen so low that the OECD, the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, has expressed alarm and regret that Canada's aid has significantly declined.
Children are the most affected because the weakest are the first to suffer and die when aid is withdrawn from Third World countries. This government has reduced its ODA expenditures by $4.5 billion since it came to power.
Third, this government is in the process of a further 10 per cent reduction. These reductions were started in the 1992-93 year and are carried into the 1993-94 estimates.
Private Members' Business
These cuts are expected to amount to about $650 million over two years.
Fourth, in addition to the funding cuts, this government has developed plans to redirect ODA funds away from the Third World especially from the least developed countries which most need long term assistance.
Instead, the government wants to use ODA funds for trade development activities in the former Soviet bloc and elsewhere. Canadian aid to the Soviet bloc is essential, but it should not be done at the expense of ODA to poorer countries. It would be much more logical to look for those funds in our defence budget or from the private sector which will profit from it in the long run.
This government, as part of its funding cuts, is reducing the assistance channelled through non-government organizations. In 1993-94 these cuts run as high as 12 per cent for some NGOs. The average across the board is about 10 per cent we are told.
Many of these funds are matching grants to NGOs which are the agencies through which tens of thousands of Canadians become directly involved in international development.
The NGOs work as partners with the local groups in developing countries. Together they work to improve basic health care, education, nutrition, farming techniques, small business operations and a host of other enterprises.
NGOs are experienced, efficient and accountable. Women and children will suffer most from this reduction to the non-government organizations.
Sixth, the government has announced that it is abruptly ending Canada's bilateral assistance programs in east Africa and the Horn of Africa. Countries like Ethiopia, Somalia, Uganda and Sudan are some of the countries which most need development and where children are suffering and dying in the largest numbers. This is part of CIDA's reduction of aid.
Seventh, the United Nations report on development has pointed out that less than 10 per cent of Canada's aid is humanitarian. Less than 10 per cent of our aid is directed toward human priorities such as clean water, basic health care, primary education and family planning.

April 2, 1993
Private Members' Business
This works out to less than $300 million out of $2.7 billion being spent on ODA actually reaching the poorest people. The poorest people are supposed to be the main target of Canadian assistance. That is what we said when we adopted Sharing Our Future.
Eighth, Canada has supported generously the international financial institutions, but it has done it without demanding from those institutions any conditions which would ensure that the projects supported by the World Bank and its regional partners would be people friendly. As a result, many World Bank projects have increased devastation and malnutrition among those affected or displaced by the many projects which the World Bank seems to favour.
Instead, these offices along with industrial countries have increased Third World debt to the point where that debt is the greatest single deterrent to progress and development in many countries. It is ironic that those loans which were supposed to be such a great help have turned out to be the greatest deterrents to development.
To Canada's credit, we have unilaterally forgiven much of our direct debt to the least developed countries in the Francophonie and the Commonwealth.
The New Democratic Party of Canada believes that the basis of all aid of all kinds should lead to the empowerment of the people of recipient countries and should lead to their self-sufficiency and independence.
Canada and all donor countries should avoid the tendency to exploit aid as internal economic development tools. Aid can be mutually beneficial without being exploitive of the recipient. Official Development Assistance is the key to giving the world's children a hopeful chance for a full life.
The New Democratic Party of Canada would immediately move to increase the effectiveness and quality of Canada's official development assistance. First, we would conduct a thorough review of ODA policy. We would ask Canadians in all walks of life, recipient countries and other donor countries to be part of a review. We would call on the considerable expertise of the NGO community and the United Nations agencies to contribute to the new policy. Farm groups, small businesses and co-ops would also be involved.
I do not suppose we would greatly change the aims of our future but we would spend a lot of time making sure that we could fulfil those aims. NGOs and other political groups have also called for such a review and rededication of Canada's aid.
Second, the New Democratic Party of Canada would immediately move to improve the quality and quantity of Canadian aid that goes into humanitarian priorities such as clean water, sanitation, nutrition, education and family planning. Those are the projects which affect women and children the most. Such a move could be made without increasing Canada's deficit.
This shift to humanitarian priorities would be best implemented by increasing our utilization of NGOs, non-government organizations. As indicated earlier, the NGOs are the most effective and efficient providers of this kind of aid since their projects are usually working directly with people and partners to help them develop their skills and ability to provide for themselves as far as possible.
This is probably the ultimate manifestation of the statement: "Give a man a fish and you feed him for a day; teach a man to fish and you feed him for life". In the Third World statistics show that women provide 85 per cent of sustenance. We can make this shift to better quality without increasing the Canadian deficit.
Third, the New Democratic Party has always supported the movement of the level of ODA to the United Nations level of 1 per cent of Gross National Product. This government has reduced the level of Canada's contribution to below .4 per cent of GNP. With this year's cuts and future dilution by making the international assistance envelope cover non-ODA countries, it is likely to drop to .3 per cent of ODA. This neglect and undermining of Canada's position is going to make it exceedingly difficult for any future government to regain this lost ground in view of Canada's national debt. New Democrats would move to turn the trend around immediately in an attempt to reach the UN target as soon as possible.
Fourth, the New Democratic Party would review Canada's contribution to IFIs, the international financial institutions, and make our continuing involvement with those institutions dependent and conditional upon policy changes which would make the World Bank institutions

April 2, 1993
much more sensitive to the humanitarian impact of any project on ordinary people.
Five, democracy means involving people. The New Democratic Party would aim its aid at the empowerment of people. The first step in this process would be the establishment of an advisory board for CIDA. Such a board would include representations from the recipient countries that would take part, and would take part in the general review of Canada's ODA policy. Such a board may extend its personnel to have smaller boards within regions in which CIDA now operates. Such a board would call heavily upon the development community in Canada: the NGOs, the business community, academia and the churches.
Aid to poor countries has been motivated in the past, as Betty Plewes of the CCIC, the Canadian Council of International Co-operation, stated: one part altruism-humanitarianism and four parts geo-political self-interest in the context of the cold war. As Betty points out, aid will probably go on being motivated by many intangibles.
Dr. Mahbub ul Haq, author of the UN development report, told a parliamentary committee last year that 95 per cent of the children born were born in Third World countries and 5 per cent were bom in industrialized countries, which is the western countries including the Soviet bloc.
Dr. Mahbub ul Haq went on to say: "The threat to you Canadians will come not from ideological differences but from poverty. Industrialized countries are a shrinking minority of the world's population. You 5 per cent of the world's people will have to deal with the 95 per cent in developing countries. You can stop poor people at your borders but you cannot stop poverty from spreading in the form of drugs, pollution and terrorism".
We committed ourselves and Canada's resources to the children of Canada and the world. We cannot separate the welfare of the world from that of Canada. Doing all we can to make the children of the world healthy, productive and content would be a good start to a better world.
Canada's efforts to alleviate poverty among children of the world is slipping. We need to recognize that and do
Private Members' Business
something about it. We need to improve the quality of our aid. We need to utilize the best people to develop that humanitarian aid. In other words, we need to work at making the children of the world citizens who can produce and benefit and be part of a good world tomorrow.

Madam Speaker, I rise in support of the proposed motion before us today for a number of reasons.
First, it is one step toward eradicating child poverty not only here in Canada but elsewhere around the world. Every one of us has a responsibility and a role to play. If we look at the future of Canada we cannot help but say: "If we cannot take care of our children today, how can we take care of the future of Canada tomorrow?" Children are the future of this country.
It is quite alarming that child poverty has hit an all-time high in Canada. During the 1980s we had approximately 984,000 living below the poverty line. In 1990, 10 years later, the number of people living below the poverty line is in excess of 1.1 million, which is about a 17 per cent increase over the past 10 years.
If we examine all the government policies over the past 10 years, and especially regarding child poverty, we can say in all fairness that we have failed on that front.
When we talk about child poverty we talk about poverty in general. A child is poor because he comes from a poor family. Poverty hits the single mothers hardest. According to Statistics Canada, 80 per cent of poor mothers have no high school diploma, and because they live below the poverty line their children are poor.
A lot of people believe that poor people normally do not work. That is totally unfair and untrue because according to statistics two-thirds of all poor in Canada whether they are poor families or a single parent are actually working poor.
According to 1990 statistics provided by Statistics Canada, 27 per cent of poor families work full time and another 40 per cent work part time. Only one-third of those poor families do not work at all because of lack of opportunities, because of disabilities or because of other considerations. That applies also to single people. More than 67 per cent of people under the age of 25 are also working poor and only about 27 per cent of those youth are not working.

April 2, 1993
Private Members' Business
Child poverty is an issue that concerns us all because poverty has a direct impact on the health of the nation. The reason why I say that is that if you look at children who live below the poverty line you will find that 40 to 50 per cent of those children were most likely born with low birth weight, with permanent growth retardation or restriction. There is a correlation between the health of the child and the quality of nutrition that he or she is receiving.
Also, when we talk about children who are poor, you will find that they are twice as likely to die before their first birthday. They experience a 50 per cent higher death rate than the average child. They are more than twice as likely to suffer long-term disabilities and other health problems. That is when we talk about poverty in general in Canadian society.
Child poverty is worse in our society when it comes to aboriginal people. If you look at the statistics going back to 1984, there was twice the number of youth or infant mortality among aboriginal people than in the average population of Canada. Furthermore, the aboriginal suicide rate in the age bracket 15 to 19 is almost seven times the rate of other children in the rest of Canada.
There is a direct correlation between poverty and what it has to do with the over-all health of the nation and what it has to do with the over-all future of the nation. A lot has been said about this issue.
Canada signed the United Nations Convention on the Right of the Child in 1990. The government is to be commended on that because it was a positive step forward that everyone has to recognize. We, on the Liberal side, are proud of the fact that Canada was one of the signators of that convention. Like anything else in life, however, unless you put laws into action and unless you take action, all of these words and promises will remain as promises.
Actions speak louder than words. So far, unfortunately, we have not seen a progressive action plan being put in place to deal with child poverty. As a matter of fact, we only have to look to the past to see that if this House unanimously adopted a motion by the year 2000 we would eradicate child poverty, but as I have indicated to you from Statistics Canada information child poverty over the past 10 years has been increasing, not decreasing.
There are things we must look at. We must develop legislation which expresses a positive minimum standard of care rather than negative prohibitions on parental behaviour. We must develop strategies to ensure that children taken into care receive the services they need and do not suffer from government neglect. We must look at ways to address this whole question in a cohesive manner rather than just dealing with it on an ad hoc basis.
Our party has come forward with a number of recommendations. I would like to cite a few of them that came as a result of the collective work of our critic for health and welfare from Winnipeg and our spokesperson on child poverty who is also from Winnipeg. They have recommended eight different steps that the government can take in order to deal with child poverty.
First the federal government should immediately participate with provincial and territorial governments through boards of education and in conjunction with community volunteers to provide nutritionally balanced breakfast, lunch and snack programs in schools throughout Canada. We know this will not solve the problem in the long term, but at least it is one first step that the government should look at.
Also the Liberal Party recommends that the government redesign the tax system to make it more equitable, to help families cope with the added expenses of raising children and simplifying the federal child benefits system. Everything boils down to income and expenses. The Liberal Parly has moved forward to recommend that the government immediately announce its intentions to have accelerated job creation programs for students to be put in place for summertime employment.
These are some of the recommendations. I can see we are pretty well running out of time. It is Friday afternoon and I do not want to monopolize the time of my other colleagues who want to speak on this issue. However I am grateful to say that the House of Commons has unanimously adopted the resolution I introduced on behalf of my party recognizing November 20 as child day in Canada.
I will read that for the record. It says that throughout Canada each and every year November 20, being the day in the year 1989 when the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child was adopted in the United Nations General Assembly, shall be known as the National Day of the Child.
April 2, 1993

This day was designated in order to allow Canadians from coast to coast on an annual basis to celebrate the potential of children, to celebrate what childhood is all about. At the same time, that day will give us a chance to assess how far we have come as a society in dealing with child poverty and what we have done as a society in order to attack the poverty that faces children.
I know there is not one single action any government can take that will solve all of the problems, but every single step could help. We have a responsibility at every level, from the school board level, municipal level and provincial level to the federal government level, to collectively set up an action plan that will help us deal with the question of today and the question of tomorrow.
To that extent I want to put on the record that we support the motion proposed by our colleague.

Madam Speaker, I too would like to speak in support of Motion No. 616, introduced by our colleague from Saskatoon-Humboldt. I thank him for his initiative.
In December 1991 the Liberal Party introduced a minority report on child poverty entitled "A Child Investment Strategy". It was introduced by my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre and myself as the health critic for the Official Opposition.
My colleague from Ottawa Centre has already alluded to some of the recommendations. I thought I would just remind the House that in the report we indicated that:
We believe that the committee's report should have called for a child investment strategy that would have marked the beginning of a 10-year campaign against all child poverty in Canada. Even within that context, the committee neglected such obvious problems as education and training -perhaps the most solid investment we can make in our children.
Then we went on to note that the Subcommittee on Poverty failed to inform the House of Commons of the extent to which federal government policies since 1984 have directly and dramatically increased poverty in every region and city throughout Canada.
In contrast to the recommendation of that committee which only urges provincial and territorial governments
Private Members' Business
to promote nutritionally balanced breakfast, lunch and snack programs in schools throughout Canada, the Liberal Party felt that we should immediately participate with those governments in implementing those nutritionally balanced breakfast, lunch and snack programs for schools throughout Canada.
I should also add that I published an article in The Medical Post about giving nutritional supplements to pregnant women who are poor. If we spent about $155 million on these pregnant women throughout the country we would have a return of about $350 million in savings by preventing 6,000 babies from being bom underweight.
We have had a long commitment to alleviating the plight of our children, to the development of our children. In that Liberal minority report of December 1991 we also indicated to Parliament and Canadians our party's commitment to full employment.
I was just reading a summary of achievements by this government from 1984 to 1993, which was published in February of this year. I would like to quote from the section on this government's contribution to world peace and development. It says:
Canada has an enviable international reputation as a responsible nation dedicated to the ideals embodied in the United Nations Charter. Canada has vigorously pursued the cause of international peace and development over the last eight years with a host of initiatives and programs.
While we applaud those initiatives that help the poor children in the world we have noted that the amount of aid to those developing countries has diminished.
I would like to submit that it is in the best interests of Canadians to help children in developing countries become strong, healthy and productive citizens, as we do for our own children and youth in Canada. Then those children in the developing countries will move the economies in their countries, and thus those countries would require imports from Canada thereby helping our economic development. Also, and this is very important, we will restore human dignity to all children of the world.

April 2, 1993
Private Members' Business
On that note I would like to reaffirm my support for the principles embodied in this motion. I reaffirm:
That in the opinion of this House, the government should make the declaration and plan of action of the World Summit for Children, held at the United Nations on the 29th and 30th of September, 1990, an integral part of Canadian international co-operation policy;
That the government should consider fully implementing the major global commitments agreed to by the 71 heads of state and government attending the summit, including domestic and international co-operation strategies for child survival and development;
That the government should consider making available adequate financial resources for these purposes, including a contribution to the additional resources required from donor countries based on Canada's historical 5 per cent of global foreign aid;
That multinational institutions be directed to focus their efforts on the implementation of summit promises;
That the minister responsible for the summit follow-up be invited to report to Parliament once a year on the implementation of the World Summit for Children plan of action and the Convention on the Rights of the Child to the extent that the application of the plan and convention, at the national, regional and international levels, requires action or a contribution on the part of Canada; and
That parliamentarians around the world be invited to ensure that each country provides its fair share of the additional resources required to see that the promises of the World Summit for Children become a reality.
I would like to leave this debate with one very important principle as we commit ourselves to these declarations by my hon. colleague from Saskatoon- Humboldt, which I support very strongly. It is the so-called first principle.
When the financial resources of Canada are plentiful let us think of our children and youth first. When the resources of the country are scarce the children and youth should suffer last.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise this afternoon to take part in this debate on motion M-616 presented by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Humbolt. As we know, I was vice-chairman of the Standing Committee on External Affairs in 1986-87 and I had the pleasure of working with other members of this House on an in-depth study regarding assistance to developing countries. I can tell you that I am well aware of what is going on, particularly with regard to African countries.
I had the pleasure of visiting several projects managed by Canada in co-operation with non-governmental organizations and I understand why Canada is reluctant to get involved in the issue of children's rights. I understand in a sense, but in another sense I do not. I understand because Canada's debt is enormous and theoretically we cannot afford to increase our financial aid to developing countries. But there are other ways to help those countries, and I find it sad because if I remember well it was our Prime Minister who chaired the World Summit for Children and it is that same Prime Minister who is now taking so much time to respond. He should give leadership and Canada should give leadership and fulfil the promises that have been made.
It is really unfortunate because today other countries are watching Canada that who was then a leader explaining to other countries what they should do in order to protect the rights of the child. That same Prime Minister does not do a thing. I wonder how Canada is now perceived after we made such a great fuss about the World Summit for Children and worked so hard to make it happen.
Let me tell again about those countries I had the opportunity to visit and about projects in those countries, most particularly in Africa. I did not get the chance to travel to other countries to see our assistance projects. In Africa we visited Tanzania, Senegal, Cameroon, Niger and Ethiopia. We made two visits to those developing countries to try and find a better way, to help them.
We realized that 30 years ago when we started to help those developing countries we tended to have a colonial approach. We wanted to help them, but we also wanted to help ourselves. We would undertake projects, always thinking that they would bring benefits to us. That has been the great tragedy. All the time we helped them, we were thinking of ourselves first. Of course, they got some assistance but it was a bad start because when you want to help yourself before you help others you forget the essential part, that is to help a country on the basis of its potential. In developing countries, particularly African countries, we developed great projects that they were unable to manage. A few years later everything was in shambles.
April 2, 1993

Let me list a few if I may. In Tanzania, for example, the Clark government found an outstanding potential for wheat production. Of course, they have some difficulty with wheat in Tanzania, but the then Prime Minister, the member for Yellowhead, accepted to develop a great wheat production project. Being a westerner, he was quite open to that kind of project and he knew very well this kind of development. He also thought that it could eventually help people in western Canada because they could sell equipment, for example. To make a long story short, we developed a great wheat production project in Tanzania, and I have to admit it was a success from the point of view of productivity and the volume of production. We developed that project much like we do in western Canada, with big farms, big tractors and big combines. We built garages to maintain this machinery and trained people to repair those tractors and combines. Everything was fine. This means there might be a hundred people working for this big project which pays quite a bit. What we forgot is that we could have gone with small NGOs or collaborative projects, which would have cost a lot less and would have employed more people. Thousands of people could have worked to produce about the same result. They would have learned to grow things. They would have acquired the know-how from our people. They would have had an opportunity to earn their living in an honourable way. They would have learned to cultivate. By doing it for them did we really help them? This is the question one must ask. Yes, we probably helped them, but not in the long term.
A few years later when this project was running smoothly Prime Minister Trudeau visited Tanzania. He went to Dar es Salaam and told them: "You are producing a lot of wheat, my friends. Dar es Salaam is a city of about two million people. It seems you are lacking a bakery". What did Mr. Trudeau do? He said we are going to build a bakery. And he built the most modern bakery of the time. What happened then? By producing large quantities of bread in that ultra-modem bakery we put all the small bakers out of business, the thousand of bakers who had worked at feeding the people of Dar es Salaam. We took away their jobs. We took away their capacity to earn an honest living.
Government Orders
Even worse, we did not put into place the maintenance infrastructure for this bakery, and the last time I went to Tanzania it was no longer operational. But between the time it started and the time it stopped producing, all the small bakers had closed shop. Did we really help these people? What I am trying to say is that with the same amount of money we could have done a lot more had we decided to genuinely help others instead of helping ourselves under the guise of helping others. This is the thrust of my speech.

Madam Speaker, now that we are back to the amendments to the Canada Elections Act, Bill C-114, I am in the unusual situation I was in when the amendment of my friend from Saskatoon-Humboldt was put.
I agreed with my former colleague who spoke before we got into Private Members' hour. I was looking forward to some explanation for the amendment from the hon. member and whether he intends to participate now in the debate.
This raises some interesting questions again in this very fundamental change in our election laws, which will affect all Canadians and hon. members. This particular amendment, as I understand it, not having had the explanation from the hon. member who moved it, is a change in the government bill that says the deposit will

April 2, 1993
Government Orders
be $1,000. This amendment is a change from the present $200. I gather that $200 has been there for some time. Neither the government clause of $1,000 nor the amendment, as I understand it, conforms to what the Lortie commission reported in the royal commission that is the basis for this phase of election reform. It made no suggestion of a dollar amount.
I certainly have filed the $200 deposit but there is the question of whether $1,000 is too much for democracy. The $500 seems to be a little more equitable for people who may want to run. Under this law we are already changing the number of people who have to sign the papers from 50 to 100, which is most likely a good thing. The nomination papers will have to be signed by 100 electors, however the real question is whether $1,000 is just a little too much.
Perhaps the hon. member's amendment is what he considers to be a compromise between $1,000, $200 and $500 and that may be reasonable. However I did not have an explanation from the member. This is an interesting question, but then we get into this whole other area of $1,000 to be allotted to third parties for advertising.
I gather from what the government House leader said earlier, the issue interests a lot of Canadians, especially Canadians who are not in this Chamber but certainly not the three registered parties in this Chamber, the Conservatives, the Liberals and the NDP. As I said, there were hon. members doing the committee report. I read what the Lortie commission said about third party advertising and trying to weigh the question of free speech. It makes sense that members and parties have restrictions on expenses. Yet third parties can come in under the present law as it has been interpreted by the courts and flood the airwaves, newspapers and post office boxes of electors if there is no restriction or limitation on the amount a third party can spend.
I do not know if I want the tax system they have in the States or these political action committees that pervert almost all the laws for election expenses. I think in most cases they are supposed to have a $5,000 limit, so they just create another committee. They can have a multitude of committees to get around their election expense laws which are really pretty horrific in terms of not really
setting any limits. Thank God it has not happened here yet, but money in the United States is almost fundamental. Unless one has millions of dollars do not even think of running for an election. Certainly in the House of Representatives one needs hundreds of thousands of dollars and in the Senate in the United States it is in the millions. I forget one of the figures but I think $2.4 million was the average for Senate races. Some people spend that much in the primaries.
Fortunately we in Canada have not quite been devoured by the need for dollars for a person to participate in our political system. This comes back to the amendment of my hon. friend that $500 sounds more reasonable than the $1,000 that is in the present bill.
We do not have the numbers to put this or so many of the amendments this afternoon to a vote. I think this is a veiy poor reflection on the whole state of Parliament. On a quiet Friday afternoon before a long break we bring in this type of legislation where there is a lot of public interest in some of these areas that affect the people and the body politic out there. Yet we have a perfunctory debate under our rules at this stage in our debate and there are not enough members to actually force a vote on some of the amendments. A lot of this is going to slip by. Members who should be taking an interest are not here and the people really do not know where they stand.
Fortunately, with extended hours today we will perhaps conclude report stage, which we are on now, because we have fairly tight limits on it and I understand that. It helps move bills along as it should.
This is where we get the problem of reform of the rules to help governments move legislation along. Understandably from a government point of view on a quiet afternoon you can get a contentious bill really sliding along. Frankly, if there had not been a few members around here today, I imagine this whole bill on electoral reform might have gone through the report stage and by unanimous consent third reading and the whole thing would be over perhaps without even a cry of division.
There may have been a cry. The member for Kingston and the Islands who has been very active in this whole
April 2, 1993

process of electoral reform and working on the committee says that at least there would be a cry of division.
As far as I am concerned, as long as there is going to be a vote on third reading, some of my interest on some of these amendments pales. I do not really have that much conviction on whether it is right or wrong. As I said, I think the government bill is better than some of the amendments. The problem is that in terms of the multitude of members in this thing, there is not the process to have members vote on something that gets pretty fundamental and to the core, and this is one.
I understand from the newspapers that some parties are concerned, those that can give tax receipts like the Rhinoceros Party and the Green Party. They can give tax receipts because they had 50 candidates in the last election. They are very concerned about this $1,000 deposit. In effect, if they had to put a $1,000 deposit into all the 295 ridings, this would be a very onerous financial burden that they might not be able to meet.
As an Independent, certainly as a Conservative member, even as a Liberal member, and probably even as an NDP member, I would most likely be happy as the devil to say that $1,000 should be the deposit because then you will not have as many so-called fringe candidates. Sitting where I am now as an Independent, I cannot really say they are any more fringe than perhaps some people might say that I am a fringe candidate. Therefore, I come down on the side of my friend's amendment even though he did not explain it.
That is what I really am disturbed about because at least he is here. I really think he owes it to the House to explain what he is trying to do because I may have misinterpreted what he is trying to do.
Again, there is an issue here that the House should divide on at the right time to see where we all stand on it. But I also understand the realities of life at 3.55 on a Friday afternoon with the number of members here and the rules. We most likely will not have a division on this matter, which I think is pretty important.
I hope I have not misinterpreted the member from Saskatoon-Humboldt who moved the motion. I think it is laudable and I would like to support it if I interpreted it correctly.

Madam Speaker, I thought Motion No. 13 was self-explanatory.

After hearing the member for Annapolis Valley-Hants I recognize that it is. That is the exact reason behind the motion that $1,000 seems a little extreme for some people and $500 is a compromise figure.
However, I want to spend another minute on the second motion, Motion No. 15. It really is much more significant than the change from $1,000 to $500 because it suggests that the total amount is returned when the official agent files the costs after the election.
The present bill suggests that candidates get half of it back when it is filed and half later if they get more than 15 per cent. In other words, if candidates do not get 15 per cent, they lose half of it. Our concern was that the candidates should get it all returned to them when they file their official returns after the election.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, once again I am pleased to rise and participate in the debate on the bill on electoral reform.
I remember the Prime Minister said that a reform of the electoral process was needed. I had the opportunity to discuss the bill on electoral reform on a few occasions with Pierre Lortie whom I have known for about 20 years because we were both members of the Chambre de Commerce des Jeunes of Montreal at the time.

April 2, 1993
Government Orders
Mr. Lortie told me on several occasions that the reform would make the Elections Act more democratic so that people would have a stronger voice in the process. That was the mandate given to his commission.
I find the debate we are involved in a bit absurd since the suggestions, the amendments and the whole bill are in complete contradiction with the commission's mandate whose thrust was to put more democracy into the electoral process to allow individuals to express themselves, with nothing to do with financing by large corporations or unions but to give the ordinary citizens a voice in the process.
Once again it is suggested that the deposit requested from the candidates be raised from $250 to $1,000. This seems to me to be contrary to this kind of freedom of speech we are looking for. I mean that $1,000 is a fair amount of money for some people or even for a young political party. As my colleague said a few minutes ago, many political parties are established with no intention of forming a government. In fact, we, the Bloc Quebecois, do not want to form a government; all we want to do here in Ottawa is to defend Quebec's interests and we want to act freely without the shackles of a Canadian national party which would silence us. We want to be able to speak freely.
We know the meaning of freedom of speech. When the people can speak freely, things begin to change. So, as a political party, we do not want to come to power, we want Quebecers to be able to express themselves freely in Ottawa. We think that power is greater when we can speak freely instead of being caught within the establishment or stuck in a caucus where everything is confidential.
Again, if political parties have to pay $1,000 the small parties will not be able to express themselves since the candidates will often not have the necessary $1,000 deposit that would allow them to run in an election here in Ottawa.
Speaking of freedom of speech, even if I do not like to make comparisons, it reminds me of the day Mr. Gorbachev-who has been in Canada for a few days-allowed his people to speak freely. As you will know, freedom of speech did not exist in the U.S.S.R. When some one would try to speak up, he was thrown in jail. So people were given the right to speak freely.
For a number of years, we have seen the people of the U.S.S.R. express themselves as they wished. In just a few years we have witnessed incredible changes in the U.S.S.R. We saw countries become sovereign-Ukraine, Lithuania, et cetera-simply because the population was allowed to express itself freely. This is what we want to do. We want to be able to express ourselves freely, for Quebec, here in Ottawa, and it is in that sense that I say the higher we make the deposit, the more we run the risk of hindering the democratic process, because the amount becomes too high. We run the risk of not allowing the population to express itself through its representatives. This is important, Madam Speaker. It is very important, even though it may not look like it.
I find it strange. This is a very important debate. There are many amendments to discuss, yet only three members have risen. Those members are from the Bloc Quebecois.
No other member from Quebec, whether Liberal or Conservative, has debated this issue. Yet, they have been here for at least a good ten years or more and they have this democratic culture. They have learned from Rene Levesque and others about financing by individuals, about democracy and about freedom of expression. Yet they remain silent. I do not understand that. I find it very difficult to understand. I see the minister of employment is here. He has not said anything either. How come no Quebecer other than those from the Bloc Quebecois is talking? I simply cannot understand that. After all, these people would be in the best position to discuss this issue. They are in the best position to understand what goes on with electoral reform. In fact, the idea of a reform came from members representing Quebec, including the Prime Minister himself, the member for Megantic- Compton-Stanstead, and the member for Lac-Saint-Jean, who were the first ones to propose this reform. It is they who in a sense forced the government to set up a commission of inquiry which precisely proposed a more democratic reform.
We have been debating amendments for a few hours and I have yet to see a member from Quebec participate in this debate. I have not seen any member from Quebec rise. Why? Are they ashamed? Are they ashamed to express themselves and say that this does not adequately meet their wishes? I believe, as I said earlier, that they are stuck in their caucus and were told not to discuss
April 2, 1993

this issue. They are avoiding this debate because it would not be very good in Quebec. This is what is going on.
Why is it that all the Liberal and Conservative members from Quebec remain silent? It is because they are not allowed to talk. They do not have the freedom of speech. This is a clear demonstration.
The short speech I just made deals with freedom of expression. I believe that the power of a nation lies in being able to express itself. If people cannot express themselves through their elected representatives in the House of Commons or in the national assembly in Quebec, then these people do not enjoy freedom of speech. Members who are supposed to represent the people do the opposite of what the population wants them to do, as was the case with the Belanger-Campeau commission during the last referendum. Madam Speaker, you might be shocked to hear this but, unfortunately, the members who represent Quebecers in this House do not defend their interests and their needs. They do exactly the opposite of what Quebecers asked them to do during the last referendum.
Why? It is because they cannot express themselves. They are prisoners of the British parliamentary system with its party caucus structure. It is an excellent system but, unfortunately, it does not meet the needs of Quebec, which wants to enjoy freedom of speech here in Ottawa. Those members cannot speak freely because they belong to a national party in which they are forced to keep quiet because they are in a minority every time they dare say something. Since members are ambitious and want to become ministers or parliamentary secretaries they would rather obey their leader than be left out. In other words, they put their personal interests well before those of Quebecers. This demonstrates that Quebecers are not well represented here in Ottawa and their only opportunity in that respect is the Bloc Quebe-cois.

He said: Madam Speaker, the purpose of this amendment is to relax as much as possible the identification for rural voters. In many rural areas, particularly farm and forest areas and on Indian reserves, people often do not carry identification. In fact in many cases they do not even have identification because it is not of much value to them.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as for Motion No. 17 put forward by the hon. member, it looks like one of those motions-he has a number of them-intended to make it easier for anyone who wants in good faith to exercise the right to vote in an election, to do so. It was also the case when he moved a motion on non-limitation with regard to the number of political parties, by imposing strict basic requirements such as a $1,000 deposit in every electoral district to have someone represent the party. The same thing with the motion on prisoners that we discussed earlier.
In this case the idea is to provide members of certain cultural communities who are not in the habit of carrying on them several i.d. cards which they could produce if need be at the time of an election or at any other time a
convenient means of identification. In that sense, the proposed amendment shows the closed mind and lack of good will this government has once more exhibited. An open-minded approach would be to allow Canadians from certain native communities or local communities where everybody knows everybody, as we were saying earlier, who are coming to vote in good faith not to produce identification. These people could exercise their right as it is exercised as democratically as possible in normal countries. Are we normal? Of course, we are. We have our faults, but we have also had the opportunity to right a few wrongs. I notice the hon. member for Lotbiniere. I could see him support such an approach as a man of the law.
But he remains silent and, more likely than not, he will decline commenting on that. Yet with his talent as a speaker and his expertise as a lawyer he could give a voice to these people in this place and express their wishes as the member representing his riding. I think that there are even native communities in his riding that he is in contact with. There are also communities which would like to hear his advice and see him stand up for them here in this House to get the right to vote without meeting 100 per cent of the requirements of the old Elections Act. The proposals submitted are not geared toward liberalizing the right to vote, but rather limiting it. This is not a precautionary measure, contrary to what we may think.
I do not think that anyone will have anything to say against this, seeing that no one on the other side has requested to speak after me to challenge my position and that of the distinguished member from the New Democratic Party who has eloquently introduced these amendments. This amendment is also in keeping with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Nothing in the charter says that we have to carry around five i.d. cards, or a single one as a matter of fact, and to sign an affidavit in order to be allowed to exercise our democratic right to vote.
The Charter of Rights and Freedoms leans toward open-mindedness instead. As we hear in court sometimes, it is better to let a dozen guilty people walk than to send one innocent person to prison. Perhaps we should err on the side of open-mindedness sometimes concerning who has the right to vote and who does not, and let one person cheat so dozens and dozens of voters are not
April 2, 1993

refused the right to participate in the democratic process.
We know why the government is once again opposed to it. It is trying to limit the democratic process in Canada because it serves its interests. Fewer ordinary people will vote, but more rich people will vote and the bigger will be their financial contribution. The government will then be in a better position to defend the interests of rich people instead of those of the majority who cannot always present identification cards when they go to the court house, the polling station, the convenience store, etc.
I appreciate very much this idea suggested by the member because it is forward looking. It is very forward looking as far as electoral legislation is concerned because it is based on the degree of tolerance and confidence which Canadians must have towards each other as well as Quebecers, and also Canadians and Quebecers, especially considering what will happen over the next two years, which will certainly result in a new economic agreement between the two countries sharing the same border.
Therefore, it is very important to establish that confidence at the individual level, as it will be important to establish it as a notion later on. This degree of trust begins when we go to the polls and have to chose between different parties, different candidates: the Tory Party that wants to serve the privileged, the Liberal Party that has not found its calling, the New Democratic Party completely out of touch with its obsolete theories; and next to them in Quebec a group of enthusiastic people with a new vision of their nation's future, of their people's future and a new vision of their relations with the rest of Canada.
Voters then have a real choice, and the choice will be easy in Quebec, of course. People will vote massively for the Bloc Quebecois. Why? Because their candidates want to serve the best interests of Quebec in Ottawa, and they want to do it as long as Quebecers will pay taxes, before going back to manage their own affairs. In that sense, to be able to vote for one of the options I mentioned is the most vital act in democratic life.
Again, as my hon. colleague for Longueuil has rightly and eloquently pointed out a few moments ago, it is a pity to see Tory members so absent from the debate. I do not mean absent from the House, it is their right, and
Government Orders
some of them are here today, but I deplore the fact that those present remain silent in such a crucial debate, a debate on electoral reform. Indeed, on November 17, five days before election day, the Prime Minister had formally committed himself to electoral reform, to an in-depth reform in order to make the democratic process more relevant and more easily accessible to disadvantaged people. The amendment put forward is a good example.
Of course, grassroots financing would have been a major reform, the second part of the reform that the House leader was saying will come after the election. When we talked about Motion No. 2 a few moments ago, the hon. member for Gatineau spoke very eloquently on that subject but he has not said a word since. He should speak again about the rights of people who would want to have access to the democratic process. Since he belongs to one of the beautiful minorities that we have in Canada and in Quebec, he would certainly be able to tell us that in some communities it is not customary for people to carry identification papers with them at all times. It would be sad to deprive certain groups of people of their right to vote, which is the ultimate expression of democracy, simply because they are not in the habit of canying identification papers.
The motion of the NDP member is very good and reflects the democratic vision that sustains many members in this House, the vision to improve the conditions in which we exercise our democratic right every four to five years when we elect our representatives. The fact that some people are prevented from exercising that right is contrary to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which the House leader likes to invoke so often. When he talks about the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, it is always to protect the millionaires who finance his party and not to protect the ordinary people who want to exercise their right to vote in an election. When an election is forthcoming the charter is always used to defend this or that. But when it was a matter of receiving millions, as it was the case during the referendum-$100,000 from the Bank of Montreal, $100,000 from the Royal Bank, $240,000 from the pharmaceutical industry-money was flowing in. They said then in the name of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms: My God, we must not stop corporations from donating money, to buy votes or to try to. But Canadians did not buy into that. They said no to the referendum. The same thing

Madam Speaker, I will try to be brief, but I do want to speak to this amendment. A few moments ago I was talking a lot about freedom of speech but I really think the government is going too far by saying that someone who comes to the polling station without identification will be able to vote, provided he or she is accompanied by a witness, somebody who knows him or her. I find it a bit abusive to give that kind of freedom to people since we know there are dishonest people in any society.
We know that come election time people will try to vote twice or three times, to vote in more than one riding. This of course will not happen in small villages where everybody knows everybody else. Nobody will vote two or three times in those places, but they could go and vote in another riding. To have the right to vote a person just needs to be accompanied by a witness who will attest that it is the person's real name and address. I think it is abusive. This time, I think we are giving too much freedom to voters and we are giving dishonest people a chance to cheat.
In Montreal, for example, where people do not know one another, someone could go to a polling station accompanied by a witness who would confirm his or her identity, and that person would have the right to vote without presenting any piece of identification, without proof, without having been registered on the voters' list. To me, it is really unacceptable, and quite dangerous to allow people to abuse the system.
When something is forbidden and when there are measures in place to prevent abuses we can expect to have a fair and honest society. However if we allow people to cheat very easily, we may very well end up with a society that will become increasingly dishonest. Therefore, I believe that we cannot allow that part of the bill to
pass because it gives to much freedom to voters and will allow dishonest people to abuse the system.
I know that in the Duplessis era in Quebec-and not only in Quebec but all over the industrialized world-people were very enthusiastic when they had an election. It was almost a national sport. People used to talk a lot about it in the villages, in rural areas. I grew up on a farm. My father was mayor for many years and he was involved in elections. I grew up in an environment where people just loved to talk about politics. Sometimes it would lead to heated arguments.
Still today some people have a passion for politics and they could use that freedom to vote in several ridings and in several polling stations because all they need to do is to be accompanied by somebody who will confirm their identity. It seems to me quite unacceptable and that is why I am against this government's proposal. I am even surprised to see such a proposal.
