Motion No. 18.
That Bill C-114 be amended in Clause 112 by striking out line 39
at page 62 and substituting the following therefor:
"ing or opposing, directly or indirectly and during an".
He said: Madam Speaker, this amendment is a fairly straightforward one. Under Bill C-114 advertising expenses are not allowed to be incurred by individuals in the course of an election campaign where they directly promote or oppose a particular registered party or a candidate if those advertising expenses exceed $1,000.
Motion No. 18 which I have moved seeks to amend that to prevent such advertising either directly or indirectly. I do not know how these terms will be interpreted by the courts, but the argument put forward by the chairman of our committee on electoral reform, the hon. member for Calgary West, is that direct advertising would be advertising that suggests the public vote or not vote for a candidate or for a party specifically, and that mentions the party or the candidate by name.
It is his view that indirect advertising is all other advertising. My view is that the $1,000 restriction ought to apply to both kinds of advertising during an election campaign where the advertising clearly is encouraging support for or opposition to a particular candidate or
Government Orders
party. There are good reasons for this law. I know there has been some public criticism especially by the National Citizen's Coalition of the proposal that the committee has been forward.
I mentioned this during my speech at second reading of this bill. I think the arguments put forward by the National Citizens' Coalition are fallacious. Its members have failed to recognize the fact, and most of their advertisements fail to recognize the fact, that we do have limits on the spending that is allowed by candidates and by political parties.
Given the fact that we have attempted to create something of a level playing-field where parties are restricted on what they can spend and where candidates are restricted on what they can spend, it seems to me very fair that there should be restrictions on what other persons are able to spend during the same time.
If it were not so, the parties would be able to encourage others to advertise on their behalf and thereby circumvent the restrictions that are applied to themselves. An unscrupulous candidate or an unscrupulous party organization could easily go to other organizations or to individuals and say, "please run ads supporting me or opposing those other people so that I can win my election". If you can do that and thereby get around the restrictions in the Canada Elections Act, then you might as well not have the restrictions in the act. In my view it is very important that we have very comprehensive restrictions in place on what other persons can do to advertise.
I know the National Citizens' Coalition feels it has the divine right to advertise as it sees fit and try to convince Canadians that its point of view is correct. It does, and I uphold its right to advertise. But not during an election campaign if it is going to participate in an attempt to defeat candidates or elect other candidates.
This kind of amendment goes some distance toward doing that. It is far from perfect. It is not the kind of amendment that I would have proposed had I been in the position that the government was in. But the amendment that I have moved at least imposes restrictions a little more forcefully and I urge the House to adopt it.

April 2, 1993
Government Orders

Madam Speaker, my hon. friend for Kingston and the Islands brought forward an amendment reflecting equity and fairness. How can government members say that indirect spending does not constitute interference in an election?
We have seen in the 1988 election large multinationals speak out for free trade for Canada. It was obvious to the whole country, because for a whole year the media talked about it, that the governing party was for it and the opposition parties against.
But various companies with vested interests put up huge resources to advertise everywhere, on television, on the radio and in the press, in order to convince Canadians that it was the best option for our country. They will deny having interfered in the election. That is utterly false. The amendment is simply to protect us. I repeat, Madam Speaker, no company or group, not even The National Citizens' Coalition, has the right to interfere in an election to choose members of this House.
Do the rich have the right to put up indirectly thousands and millions of dollars in order to convince the public to vote for a party because they think it knows what is best for the country? That is not right. As long as we want a political system that is truly democratic we must suppress all interference, especially that which can be used through today's media.
It seems simple enough to me. It is very simple, really. We live in a democracy that believes in fairness and justice. But if we persist in saying that some have the right to make their case in an election by putting up huge resources, in the millions of dollars, that is unacceptable. If they want to promote their option let them do it in between elections.
After an election is called, when Canadians have to elect their representatives to this House, nobody should be able to influence the electorate and nobody should avail themselves of the means to get the candidates to decide for one option or another. They should be completely free to choose, without falling prey to the propaganda in the media. We saw that in 1988. Hardly 20 minutes could go by on radio or half an hour on television without some loud advertising spot. The coverage was the same in the newspapers. This was literally brainwashing in favour of one option aimed at protecting the interests of large multinationals, as time has proven.
Even though this amendment is not agreed to today, it is only a matter of time before it becomes law because in the future, people will wonder. They will see that some members in this House who are the people's representatives have supported a measure allowing anybody to spend as much money as they want to influence the outcome of an election. They will wonder what they were thinking when they made that decision. Well, I can tell them that they do not think. They only reflect what the most affluent minority in this country thinks. This measure should have never been put forward. We should have understood that in a democratic country like ours, with our political system, this was fundamental.

Madam Speaker, I have the highest respect for the mover of this amendment, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, who I said earlier is one of the hardest working members in the House and has certainly been very involved in the committee.
However, showing my independent stance, while I have agreed with him on a couple of his amendments and disagreed with him on another one which he moved earlier today and felt more in favour of the government bill on an earlier matter, I can understand what he is trying to do on this one.
My hon. friend for Gatineau said a couple of things in his oration which really stimulated me to rise in debate. It is the very fact that we are in a democracy that this amendment gets into one of the most contentious items in this electoral reform bill. That is the right of third parties, people who are not members of a registered party, not Liberals, Tories, NDPs, Bloc Quebecois, Green, Rhinoceros and not necessarily multinationals, who just happen to be Canadians. They just may not be too happy with any of the parties, people, issues or candidates.
I give full credit to the member for Kingston and the Islands for moving this amendment because I can see he is trying to tighten up what is in the present bill. The present bill has no logic to it in that as long as it is not directly for or against a candidate it can be an open sesame and the money can pour in, the way my friend from Gatineau explained and as happened in the 1988 election. There is no doubt big money was behind the government move for free trade. The newspapers were flooded with supplements and a lot of advertising. That
April 2, 1993

was multinational. Yes, that is an odious thing. It is the interesting red herring to move on something like this.
I just happen to have a very interesting Canadian in my riding who was basically a Liberal from a large family and very uptight on the free trade issue. I am not going to embarrass him by mentioning his name, although I do not think it would matter. He phoned me at the height of the campaign long before the multinationals became involved to try to help the polls for the Tories in the last three weeks. We all know how the polls went up and down like a roller-coaster in that 1988 campaign.
This elderly gentleman is very involved in the apple business, trucks his apples to Boston and has been doing it for years. He said: "Patrick, I am very disturbed. Yes, I used to have a heritage on the Liberal side but I believe in free trade". Quite frankly I had a lot of difficulty when I was a Conservative at that time on the free trade issue. It was the toughest election I ever fought.
I knew what free trade opened up. There was a lot of imprecise language, certainly nothing on subsidies or the question of the dispute settlement mechanism. One turkey producer in Pennsylvania produces more turkeys than all of Canada. It is the same for the vertical integration of some of the chicken farms in Arkansas, to mention a state that has become famous recently, and/or in the deep south. It makes our chicken production pale by comparison.
My farmers were very concerned about free trade, about having an open floodgate. In any event I fought the fight. I supported the party line and I had difficulty. This gentlemen wanted to put an ad in the paper and he put it.
This is why this House is almost irresponsible in debating this issue on a Friday afternoon before the Easter recess when there is only a handful of us here, and other members are doing their thing. We all know we have to get home on the weekends.
Government Orders
This is an issue that should be debated by all members. We know more than the national coalition. I have no love or no hate for the national coalition. Frankly I think it does focus on a lot of interesting issues affecting Canadians.
This is an issue that affects Canadians. They may not want this closed club of parties to say they are not going to be able to spend $1,000 with some friends and put an ad in the local weekly or daily and say that they are either for or against. I know this opens up perils to candidates and to members, because then we might get the single issue candidates. Let us forget about the multinationals. That was free trade, and I agree with my friend from Gatineau. Who knows, it might happen again but we have other issues in Canada.
It could be abortion, pro-life or pro-choice. It could be the gun lobby. There are many different interested Canadians who because of their frustration with the political process and because they think their members are not serving them certainly do not want this Parliament to take away their right to place an ad.
The member for Kingston and the Islands is facing the issue and points a finger not at the duplicity but at the double standard in the bill that the government has brought forward.
It says that there can be a restriction on direct advertising but if it is indirect then it is wide open. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands is doing a service in that people either believe in the principle or they do not. I do not happen to believe that we should cut Canadians off from their potential choice.
For my friend from the Gatineau and members here, we are members of Parliament, members of registered parties. We have a few advantages going into an election. There is something called an incumbent advantage, an incumbent benefit. Most of us send out householders. If we do not we are rather crazy. We do that at public expense four times a year. We have free mailing privileges.
We have a lot of privileges long before the campaign begins to help plant little seeds with our constituents, our electorate, that hopefully will sprout into support during a campaign.

April 2, 1993
Government Orders
I really was quite surprised-and that is really what got me on my feet today, although I think I was going to speak on the motion anyway. Frankly I wish this House would adjourn, because then the House could come back after Easter when the House is full up with members.
On this basic issue members should stand up and speak and give their views. I respect their views. I know the Lortie commission wrestled with this. We have to wrestle with the rights of free speech and the fact that members and candidates in an election have limits.
How can we have Canadians come in the back door and get around the limit that confronts parties? My answer is that this is democracy. When I heard a colleague in this House say that no one should influence the electorate I was absolutely horrified. I do not think it was intended the way it came out, because that is the whole purpose of an election.
I will have propaganda and I will have subtle propaganda before an election through my householders, my mailings, and through keeping in touch with my riding. That is proper, and it is proper for every member here.
Goodness gracious to them. Kitty bar the door when the writ is issued and Canadians cannot do what they may want to do. The important point is one that the amendment does not address. Frankly, I wish the bill would address it and I think the Lortie commission debated it.
To me it is not the money. Yes, that could be a factor. I could fall by the wayside because of what I am saying here today, giving the potential of single interest groups to get involved in a campaign and still not be involved in a party.
Madam Speaker, you know from your experience the answer is disclosure. I think that is the matter in this proposal by the government for a hybrid restriction of no more than $1,000 for direct advertising against or for a candidate. If it is an issue then it is open season. Disclosure should be in that bill. If there is a supplement in the newspaper or an ad, they have to disclose who the people are who put the money up.
If it is the multinationals-and that has been raised as a bogeyman here; it was real in 1988,1 agree-well then okay. Canadians are not stupid.
Madam Speaker, you sat in the chair during the referendum debate when there were about six or eight of us back here who voted no on the referendum. We know what the Canadians did. We know as of yesterday or the day before, under the Access to Information Act, $7.4 million was spent for the yes side.
At least.

That is just what was admitted. It was all by big corporations.
I must say I have not really exceeded my limit too much today on this lovely afternoon. Madam Speaker, you are telling me I am almost out of time. I very glad the member for Kingston and the Islands and the member for Gatineau spoke because they got me activated and stimulated.
To me disclosure helps take care of part of the problem. The Canadian people are not stupid. They showed that in the referendum with massive advertising for yes, with the three national parties saying yes, with every political leader in this country in premierships saying yes and with the advertising heavy, the public said no.
That is the lesson I think members in this House should take to heart. They should be against any restrictions on the right of the Canadian people to get involved in their way in election campaigns.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is the worst thing I have ever seen. First of all, that does not coincide at all with the will of the Conservative Party. I will tell you why by quoting what the Prime Minister said on November 17, 1988. The Prime Minister on November 17, 1988, just before the 1988 election, was reported to have said: "An act requiring that all federal political parties rely on financing by the general public will be passed right at the beginning of the second term of the Conservative Party". That commitment was given by the Prime Minister yesterday in Montreal during an exclusive interview with La Presse."
The Prime Minister said that he wanted to promote grassroots financing. What is happening? If I were a Conservative member today I would be ashamed. On top of not proposing financing by the population, the government is allowing big companies and big unions to finance political parties and, moreover, it is allowing third parties to finance or promote political parties. The Prime
April 2, 1993

Minister said: "I want the Canadian people, each and every one, to finance political parties".
We are far from seeing that. Beside not using grassroots financing, the government is allowing third parties to support political parties. This is serious. I did not think the government would go that far. I did not think that it took Canadians and Quebecers for idiots. There is a limit to the contempt it has for people. The government is showing complete contempt for Quebecers, particularly because in Quebec we are used to financing by the population. We are accustomed to having our political parties financed by individual Quebecers and that is working quite well.
During the last referendum, we lived an experience which was rather easy to understand. We as members of the committee for the no in Quebec were financed by the people, by the voters. I can assure you that when people are determined to be heard, they will not hesitate to pull $5, $100, $200, up to $3000 out of their pockets to defend their interests and beliefs.
It is not necessary, far from it, to ask large unions and corporations to finance parties in their own interests. Government represents the people. It represents individuals and not just businesses and industries.

-in the majority for the bloc, as the member for Richelieu has just said, according to the latest polls.
It is nevertheless shameful and appalling. Truly appalling. I cannot believe what I am hearing. The Prime Minister, supported by the Conservative MPs, has taken
Government Orders
a position by saying: "At the next election, there will be grassroots financing. People will contribute to the campaign fund. That way the people's interest will be protected". This is not what is happening. As a matter of fact as I have just said it is exactly the opposite.
Similarly I said that during the referendum, which I gave as an example, the people of Quebec made a choice and financed the No Committee at the grassroots level and the results were very good.
In Longueuil, for example, we were able to collect in a relatively short period of time, in the two counties making up my riding, about $50,000 at the grassroots. The highest single contribution came from an important contractor I will not name. That was a personal contribution, not a corporate one. Those are two different things.
Besides, we have seen that the Quebec Chief Electoral Officer had serious doubts as to the acceptability of subliminal publicity proposed by the federal government and financed by large companies, especially English ones. Every minute of every day, there was publicity on television, on the radio, everywhere and, strangely, it was not accounted for in election spending.
How can the Chief Electoral Officer control election spending as long as we allow third parties to promote one party or another or one economic sector instead of another? How can the Chief Electoral Officer control spending during a campaign?
I cannot get over it, especially as a Quebecer, because these things changed in Quebec a long time ago. I cannot believe that Conservative as well as Liberal members from Quebec do not object to such a thing. It baffles me since it all started in Quebec. It is Quebec that asked the Prime Minister for reform. The Prime Minister himself mandated Pierre Lortie and his commission, known as the Lortie commission, to undertake a full review in order to make our election system even more democratic. The province of Quebec started all this. Why are there no Conservative or Liberal members from Quebec here in Ottawa who have the guts and the courage to speak? Have their caucuses really asked them to keep quiet? I think so. How could it be otherwise? They were officially ordered to say nothing about this bill. How could it be otherwise? You cannot possibly believe the opposite, Madam Speaker, because it goes against the

April 2, 1993
Government Orders
mandate the Prime Minister himself gave Pierre Lortie and his commission.
From what I see today I can understand why the country is going bankrupt. We are not logical. We have no over-all project. We always stand for personal or individual interests instead of promoting an over-all project which would allow us to go foreward. That is why the majority of Quebecers decided to withdraw from the Canadian federation. They were sick of this government in Ottawa doing stupid things and putting forward senseless projects relating to transportation, or duplication between federal and provincial departments. The same thing goes for transportation which we discussed yesterday.
Life goes on and the country is faced with a total debt of $500 billion, which is about as much as the gross national product. If you know how to count you know we are going bankrupt.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased, after the independent member from Nova Scotia and the member for Longueuil, to also say a few words on this amendment. Proposed by a Liberal member, the same member who moved a motion earlier.
This amendment is so essential to the smooth functioning of democracy in Canada that I do not understand, as my colleague the member for Longueuil was saying, how we can let it pass. Why is the government rushing this bill through, on a Friday, just before leaving for two weeks for the Easter break? The government tries to slip this by quietly, in complicity with the two other parties. Even if he moved the amendment, the Liberal member for Kingston and the Islands who is listening intently to my speech did not ask other members of his party to back it.
It is not necessary, the amendment is so good.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext:
The Liberal Party is somewhat of an accomplice to the party in office. Why does it do that? Because it does not want a vote. It is scared to vote. Because it is an accomplice it crosses to the other side. It can sit on either side of the House. It is very comfortable
because it is defending the same ideas, the same interests, that is the financial interests of privileged few.
I would like to make a comparison between clause 2 that we examined earlier this afternoon and this motion. When we talked about allowing small parties to have a showing in an election, the government kept them away by requiring a deposit of $1,000 per riding for the right to make their voices heard. That is the case of the Green Party that wanted to work for the environmental cause, of the Social Credit Party and so on. Several political parties are using election campaigns in order to force candidates to take a stand on substantive issues. That is totally contrary to the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights, article 19 more specifically that I will quote.
Article 19 says: "Everyone has the right to freedom of opinion and expression; this right includes freedom to hold opinions without interference and to seek, receive and impart information and ideas through any media regardless of frontiers".
By refusing the NDP amendment to clause 2, the government violates the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of the United Nations that Canada signed. I think that it is the Green Party's intention to ask the United Nations for a vote condemning this violation of human rights.
That is the government's position regarding the freedom of expression of small political parties. Let us now look at the amendment in terms of that freedom of expression. The amendment would limit the right of corporations to intervene by supporting a political party or, during a campaign, by paying for advertising on behalf of organizations like the coalition for something, or participate in the campaign by using unlimited advertising resources. That amendment was ignored by the government. What was its response? No, no, no. According to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, multinational companies are entitled to freedom of expression.
However, Mr. Justice Michaud in the Lipton case said that failure to limit intervention by third parties not directly involved in an electoral campaign or having private interests to protect would put democracy in serious danger. That is they intervene in the election
April 2, 1993

Government Orders
campaign to boost the chances of a certain party in order to benefit from it later on by obtaining contracts and party favours. That is where the danger lies.
The government ignored the Lortie report which did not go very far. It fails to keep the Prime Minister's commitment of November 17 and the commitments of witnesses like the hon. member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead who gave a quite exceptional testimony at the Lortie commission when he asked: "Can the workers of my riding who barely earn $15,000 a year seriously believe that an engineering firm, a large bank or a businessman can pay $50,000 to a political party without hoping for a return on their investment? Can they seriously believe that they have as much weight as those people in the decision-making process?" To ask this question is to answer it.
Why would the big multinational companies and the big consortiums nurture political parties if they did not intend to make them fat in order to have them serve their interests afterwards? In this matter Quebec has been at the forefront by being the first province and the only North American state to table a bill which prohibits any person who does not have the right to vote from financing a political party. This eliminates unions, nonprofit institutions and corporations.
The number of political contributions has increased in Quebec because political parties there have regained the support of individuals who have the right to vote. Those individuals have decided to finance them, to keep them to serve their interests. These parties now serve the interests of individuals and not those of a wealthy minority.
The Prime Minister said he understood that sentiment. On November 17 a front page article my colleague quoted from La Presse said: "Mulroney has committed himself to have the general public finance political parties. Mulroney has committed himself to put an end to all the scandals that befell the Conservative Party during its first four years in power". One of the favoured tools they are looking at is that of grassroots financing, an in depth reform of the financing of political parties. But now no mention is made of that commitment in this proposed reform. Corporations, privileged classes are allowed to take over the Conservative Party and other parties as well so they will be in a position to serve their own interests rather than the public interest.
There is no willingness to even make the change suggested in my hon. friend's amendment, Motion No. 18, whereby the vote could not be influenced directly or indirectly-and there is emphasis on the word indirectly-through major advertising and financial support to political parties partial to wealth. In that sense my colleague was right when he wondered how Quebec members in this House could turn their backs on Quebec's greatest political heritage since one of the most significant political moves world-wide was the Loi sur le financement despartis politiques allowing only voters to contribute to political parties.
This is the heritage of which we have been proud now for over 15 years, since 1977. These members should be here to ponder upon this fact and to encourage other members of their party to do the same. Unfortunately they let themselves be moulded and they fall in like sheep in this federalist line-up, oblivious to the interests of their people, their nation and their Quebec which they are supposed to protect. Fortunately, soon we will see here a group of 50, 60 individuals-men and women- willing to defend Quebec's best interests. Those who will have chosen to forget will be condemned to stay at home and spend the rest of their lives in shame and forsaken by all.

Madam Speaker, to get back to the debate, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands came back with his amendment that would prohibit third party advertising during an election campaign.
In 1988 there was an incredible amount of advertising in the various media expressing views on free trade, and it was obvious to the public that this type of advertising favoured the party in power which supported the free trade agreement as the best option for our country.
In fact there is always the risk and that is why we propose this amendment that organizations like the National Citizens' Coalition, for instance, and I do not mean this as an insult, might present an option that would not necessarily reflect the will of the majority. Because of their substantial resources they would be able to use-and we saw that in 1988 with free trade-TV, radio and the press to try and convince people that theirs is the best option for the country. That is where the danger lies. This amendment is intended to prevent that.
In an election campaign only recognized political parties should be allowed to set forth policies. If groups or individuals wish to take part in the democratic process they should belong to a political party and do their advertising within a democratic framework.
However, if individuals who are very wealthy or organizations with major resources are allowed to do this, the result may be a media blitz with an impact out of all proportion to the group's status. We always want to reflect the interests of the majority. But if minority groups have tremendous resources, it will be hard for them to understand what is happening in the process. That is why in an election campaign we must have restrictions to ensure party policy is reflected by the party honestly.
If they are allowed to call upon tremendous outside financial resources, it will skew the democratic process and that is why the hon. member's amendment proposes to avert this potential risk. Madam Speaker, the process which resulted in this bill started four years ago. It all started on April 3, 1989 in the Throne Speech at the beginning of the second session of this legislature. In the Throne Speech, His Excellency the Governor General said that his government would appoint a commission of inquiry whose mandate would be to make recommendations on changes that should be brought to the country's election.
Today we have a great bill following a study by this commission of inquiry and a year-long study of the commission's report by a committee of the House which proposed a bill greatly similar to Bill C-114.

The problem is not so much what is in this bill but what is not in it. As members of the Liberal Party and members in opposition we fought very long and hard in the Special Committee on Electoral Reform to have included in this bill various items that have been omitted.
I have moved some amendments here today which have been defeated that sought to improve the bill in so far as the bill itself went. I also tried to move two amendments which were ruled out of order which dealt with the rights of women under our electoral law. They would have enhanced the ability of women to run for public office, for membership in this House and would have provided incentives to the parties to recruit and allow them to stand as candidates. This would be with a
April 2, 1993

view to increasing the representation of women in the House. Those amendments were ruled out of order by the Chair. I can understand the ruling and I can see why they were ruled out of order.
When the committee made specific recommendations on one of those issues and the government chose to remove it from the bill, I found it difficult to understand why we are unable to move an amendment that the committee had proposed in its draft legislation and which is then out of order simply because the government bill does not include it.
Be that as it may, we have been unable to deal with those aspects of the electoral law in the course of this bill. The committee is continuing its work. When I say it is ad nauseam we do sit very long hours and have discussed this matter most extensively in committee, that and other matters.
We sat most of this past week. We did not sit today but we were sitting yesterday and I believe on Monday and Tuesday. We will be sitting on Monday when we resume. We are trying to reach agreement on various points but my general observation-I know the government House leader will probably disagree with me when I say this-is that in our view we are very concerned that the government is not really interested in electoral reform. What we are getting here is electoral fiddling.
This bill represents the culmination of work that has gone on since 1987 at least. Many of the amendments in this bill are ones that are not controversial. They will enhance our electoral law and were recommended by the chief electoral officer in his report which was tabled in this House in 1988.
We have not broken a whole lot of new ground. There are some new things: The special ballot rules are going to be a significant improvement and will broaden the franchise by allowing people who were previously disenfranchised to vote. The rules respecting the right to vote for non-resident Canadians is an improvement.
There are other things that are not improvements. We tried to get some of those fixed today with these amendments and failed. We will continue to try in the committee where we are pressing on with other matters.

We are agreeing to passage today because we believe it is in the best interest of the Canadian public to have this bill in place in time for the next election.

If he is smart and moves it on a Wednesday afternoon he can have the whole afternoon to debate it until the government moves adjournment of the debate. I invite him to do that.
As for me and my party, we have our regrets about this bill and we have made those very clear, succinctly but clearly, in the course of the debate today. I regret that this is being pushed through on a Friday afternoon and I had asked the government House leader to give time for this bill earlier in the week. Unfortunately he said he was unable to do that, which I think indicates the priority the government places on electoral reform. Nevertheless, we are faced with it today.
We have to proceed with something in order for the Chief Electoral Officer to get this in place for the next election. I think most Canadians will be well served by those provisions that will be put in place, specifically the changes relating to the special ballot rooms which will enable more Canadians to vote than has been possible in the past.

The hon. members represent Quebec. In that province the elections act already gives voters the right to vote even if they do not reside in the province. The rules are not the same for the country, and we would like all Canadians to be able to vote during a general election regardless of where they live.

I hope that all members in this House will support this bill, because it is an important measure for all Canadians. Even if we disagree over some clauses, we can still support this bill today, even though all our motions were defeated.

The hon. members in this party have their grave regrets, as I have said. We are not very happy with what is not in this bill, but we are reasonably happy with what is in it. It is only what is in it and what we might add to what is in it that we can talk about. We wish there were many other things in the bill that are not there. But given that we have what is here on this piece of paper and that is what we have to vote on today, as an opposition we are prepared to say that is what we will go ahead with. We believe it is in the best interests of Canadians even though we wish there was a lot more in it. It is not there however and we are stuck with having to proceed with what is here. We are reluctantly agreeing to this today in

order to allow for more Canadians to participate in the election, whenever it is held.
I think I speak for most Canadians when I say that we want an election at the earliest opportunity. Canadians are most anxious that there be an immediate election. Then the leadership convention my hon. friends opposite are having could be deferred to a later date. We could have the election and then they could choose their new leader.
